## Biological model equations and numerical verification — Biological model equations and numerical verification [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/
Coverage: reading

THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data
This survey selects 22 biological and biologically motivated model families,
from population growth to stochastic gene regulation and fluid–structure
coupling. It expands the equation map beyond conservation-law CFD. The 22-family survey links scoped examples of logistic growth, closed SIR, linear reaction–diffusion, linear Schnakenberg onset, finite-amplitude nonlinear evolution and post-growth 1D patterns, plus spatially uniform FitzHugh–Nagumo. This does not implement all 22 families. Separate fixed-input releases add single-cell HH current controls, immigration–death SSA, a special Fisher traveling front, 2D Schnakenberg boundary modes and a forced Keller–Segel manufactured problem. Three further fixed examples from the separate small-models group cover four-state enzyme/QSSA, a positive Lotka–Volterra orbit, and SEIR conservation with full two-mode early linearization. SEIR is separate from the existing SIR execution scope.
The equations below use conventional simplified or normalized forms. A source
identifies the model lineage, not a claim that every coefficient and variable
matches that paper. The structured catalog
retains references, numerical issues, verification targets and scope for each
entry. The selection emphasizes numerical variety, rather than a comprehensive

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — Biological model equations and numerical verification [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/
Coverage: reading

review of present-day mathematical biology. Sources checked on 6 November 2026.

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — Which biological questions exercise which algorithms# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#which-biological-questions-exercise-which-algorithms
Coverage: reading

Population growth and ecology: logistic, predator–prey, Fisher fronts,
cross-diffusion and replicator dynamics test positive states, invariant sets,
long-time behavior and spatial invasion.
Demography and epidemics: age transport and compartment models test
renewal boundaries, balances, nonnegative compartments and thresholds.
Biochemistry and metabolism: enzyme kinetics and Monod growth connect
stiff ODEs, conservation laws and reduced models.
Morphogenesis: Turing analysis, Gierer–Meinhardt, Schnakenberg and
Gray–Scott separate physical instability from numerical pattern selection.
Excitation: Hodgkin–Huxley, FitzHugh–Nagumo and Aliev–Panfilov connect
stiff reactions to pulse conduction, refractoriness and spiral waves.
Gene regulation and noise: delayed feedback, toggles, repressilators and
the chemical master equation need history interpolation, bifurcation analysis
or jump-process simulation.
Biomechanics: a fluid–elastic structure requires constitutive forces and
a coupling discretization in addition to fluid equations.
Existing diffusion and elliptic methods, FEM,
sparse/Newton methods, stiff integrators
and incompressible projection supply useful numerical
building blocks. Their current tests do not verify these new biological systems.

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — Historical model catalog# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#historical-model-catalog
Coverage: reading

Dates identify an early source or a selected development, not an exclusive
priority claim. Later spatial extensions, reductions and translations are
identified with their individual entries.

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 01 · 1838 · Logistic population growth# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#01-1838-logistic-population-growth
Coverage: reading

Logistic fixed-input / analytic checks available. Density-limited growth with carrying capacity K. It is the simplest biological ODE baseline.
\dot N=rN(1-N/K).
Numerical issue. Positivity, preservation of equilibria and overshoot of K; an accurate-looking curve can still violate the invariant interval.
Proposed verification. Compare with N(t)=K/[1+(K/N0−1)exp(−rt)] for N0>0; measure temporal order and behavior near 0 and K.
Model convention. The linked original is the later 1847 memoir; the 1838 note itself was not audited. The differential equation is not the discrete logistic map.
Sources: Verhulst, Pierre-François (1847).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 02 · 1913 · Michaelis–Menten and full enzyme kinetics# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#02-1913-michaelismenten-and-full-enzyme-kinetics
Coverage: reading

A fixed four-state enzyme/QSSA example distinguishes initial-layer, integration and reduction errors. Enzyme saturation; the full mass-action system resolves the transient complex C, while the rate law eliminates a fast variable.
E+S\mathrel{\mathop{\rightleftharpoons}^{k_1}_{k_{-1}}}C\mathrel{\mathop{\longrightarrow}^{k_2}}E+P,\qquad v=V_{\max}S/(K_M+S).
Numerical issue. Fast initial layers and stiffness; full and reduced models have different validity regimes. Under the usual quasi-steady approximation KM=(k−1+k2)/k1.
Proposed verification. Check E+C and S+C+P conservation in the closed mechanism. Compare reduced and full systems as enzyme/substrate scales vary, rather than calling the reduction exact.
Model convention. The 1913 rapid-equilibrium interpretation and the 1925 quasi-steady-state derivation must remain distinct.
Sources: Michaelis–Menten (1913; via the 2011 translation), Briggs, George E. and Haldane, J. B. S. (1925), Johnson, Kenneth A. and Goody, Roger S. (2011).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 03 · 1920 · Lotka–Volterra predator–prey# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#03-1920-lotkavolterra-predatorprey
Coverage: reading

A fixed positive Lotka–Volterra orbit has independent-reference, invariant and step-refinement comparisons. Coupled prey growth and predation; a phase-plane and long-time integration test.
\dot x=\alpha x-\beta xy,\qquad\dot y=\delta xy-\gamma y.
Numerical issue. Positive states and artificial damping or growth of closed orbits. Periodic orbits of this idealized system are not attracting limit cycles.
Proposed verification. Monitor H=δx−γ ln(x)+βy−α ln(y) for positive x,y, and compare orbit drift under step refinement.
Sources: Lotka, Alfred J. (1920), Volterra, Vito (1926).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 04 · 1926 · McKendrick age-structured population# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#04-1926-mckendrick-age-structured-population
Coverage: reading

Structured population transport · Survey only. Individuals move through age a at unit speed; newborns enter through a nonlocal renewal boundary.
\partial_t n+\partial_a n=-\mu(a)n,\qquad n(0,t)=\int_0^\infty b(a)n(a,t)\,da.
Numerical issue. Upwind/FV transport in age, birth-boundary quadrature and truncation of the infinite age interval.
Proposed verification. Use characteristic survival along cohorts and check d∫n da/dt=births−deaths, including any artificial oldest-age outflow.
Model convention. This is the classical age-transport form; the later von Foerster lineage is acknowledged without treating its date as the first appearance.
Sources: McKendrick, A. G. (1926).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 05 · 1927 · SIR and SEIR compartment models# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#05-1927-sir-and-seir-compartment-models
Coverage: reading

Closed-SIR example retained; SEIR conservation and early linearization have a separate fixed-input example. Closed, well-mixed normalized population fractions. SEIR adds an exposed compartment and a progression rate.
\dot s=-\beta si,\quad\dot i=\beta si-\gamma i,\quad\dot r=\gamma i,\quad s+i+r=1.
Numerical issue. Nonnegative compartments, invariant total population and correct resolution of epidemic peak times.
Proposed verification. Check total 1 and i+s−(γ/β)ln(s) for β>0,s>0; compare early growth rate βs0−γ and final-size relation in the closed SIR specialization.
Model convention. The original general epidemic framework is broader than this SIR specialization. Population-count and fraction conventions give different β definitions.
Sources: Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G. (1927).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 06 · 1937 · Fisher–KPP invasion front# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#06-1937-fisherkpp-invasion-front
Coverage: reading

Separate fixed-input example: Fisher–KPP: a special-speed exact front. Spatial spread of an invading population or advantageous allele, represented by a reaction–diffusion front.
u_t=D\Delta u+ru(1-u),\qquad 0\leq u\leq1.
Numerical issue. Spatial and temporal front-speed errors; leading-edge resolution, positivity and finite-domain boundary contamination.
Proposed verification. Use the Ablowitz–Zeppetella exact front at c=5√(Dr/6), or test the minimal speed 2√(Dr) only with the appropriate steep initial-data regime on a sufficiently large domain.
Model convention. Fisher–KPP is a conventional family name; the independent KPP 1937 original remains an archival follow-up. The exact special speed is not the minimal speed.
Sources: Fisher, R. A. (1937), Ablowitz, Mark J. and Zeppetella, Anthony (1979).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 07 · 1949 · Monod growth and chemostat# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#07-1949-monod-growth-and-chemostat
Coverage: reading

Biochemical reactions · Survey only. Nutrient-limited biomass X, substrate S, yield Y and chemostat dilution d; d=0 gives a closed batch model.
\mu(S)=\mu_{\max}\frac{S}{K_S+S},\quad\dot X=(\mu(S)-d)X,\quad\dot S=d(S_{in}-S)-\mu(S)X/Y.
Numerical issue. Washout near a threshold, disparate resource/growth scales, positivity and the distinction between yield and rate constants.
Proposed verification. For d=0 check S+X/Y. For d>0 use d(S+X/Y)/dt=d[Sin−(S+X/Y)] and verify the washout equilibrium.
Model convention. This writes one constant-yield extension of saturation growth, not a universal metabolic model.
Sources: Monod, Jacques (1949).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 08 · 1952 · Hodgkin–Huxley membrane dynamics# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#08-1952-hodgkinhuxley-membrane-dynamics
Coverage: reading

Separate fixed-input example: Hodgkin–Huxley: clamps, rest and firing. Voltage and gating variables z=m,h,n describe an ionic excitable membrane. A cable extension adds spatial axial current.
C_m\dot V=I_{app}-\bar g_{Na}m^3h(V-E_{Na})-\bar g_Kn^4(V-E_K)-g_L(V-E_L),\quad\dot z=\alpha_z(V)(1-z)-\beta_z(V)z.
Numerical issue. Stiff gates, removable singularities in rate formulas, gating bounds, voltage/current sign and temperature conventions.
Proposed verification. Select an explicitly versioned CellML/reference convention, verify resting equilibrium and gate relaxation at clamped voltage, then refine spike time and waveform.
Model convention. The original squid-axon model is not a calibrated human cardiac model. No single rate parameter set is selected by this survey.
Sources: Hodgkin, A. L. and Huxley, A. F. (1952).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 09 · 1952 · Turing reaction–diffusion framework# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#09-1952-turing-reactiondiffusion-framework
Coverage: reading

Separate scoped checks of linear onset, nonlinear evolution and post-growth patterns for fixed 1D Schnakenberg systems. A framework for diffusion-driven pattern onset around a homogeneous reaction equilibrium, not a unique choice of f and g.
u_t=D_u\Delta u+f(u,v),\qquad v_t=D_v\Delta v+g(u,v).
Numerical issue. Physical versus numerical instability, domain eigenmodes and errors in the discrete Laplacian dispersion relation.
Proposed verification. For a selected kinetic law compare eigenvalues of J−k²diag(Du,Dv) with early-time Fourier-mode growth. Show that the k=0 reaction equilibrium is stable before asserting diffusion-driven instability.
Model convention. A spot image or unequal diffusion coefficients alone do not establish a Turing mechanism. Boundary conditions determine the available modes.
Sources: Turing, Alan M. (1952).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 10 · 1961 · FitzHugh–Nagumo excitation and recovery# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#10-1961-fitzhughnagumo-excitation-and-recovery
Coverage: reading

FHN excitation/recovery ODE and time checks retained. Single-cell HH has a separate fixed case; spatial axons and experimental calibration remain unvalidated. A normalized fast excitation/slow recovery model for pulses, refractoriness and spiral waves when extended in space.
v_t=D\Delta v+v-v^3/3-w+I,\qquad w_t=\epsilon(v+a-bw).
Numerical issue. Stiff time-scale separation, splitting error, wave-speed convergence and numerical wave breakup.
Proposed verification. Check ODE fixed points/nullclines and small-perturbation eigenvalues first; then refine a 1D pulse before a 2D spiral movie.
Model convention. This is a common normalized variant; cubic coefficients, recovery signs and nondimensionalization differ between formulations.
Sources: FitzHugh, Richard (1961), Nagumo, Jinichi and Arimoto, Suguru and Yoshizawa, Shuji (1962).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 11 · 1970 · Keller–Segel chemotaxis# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#11-1970-kellersegel-chemotaxis
Coverage: reading

Separate fixed-input example: Keller–Segel: a manufactured coupled-flux solution. Cell density n drifts up a chemoattractant gradient; τc=0 gives an elliptic chemical subproblem.
n_t=D_n\Delta n-\chi\nabla\cdot(n\nabla c),\qquad\tau_c c_t=D_c\Delta c+\alpha n-\lambda c.
Numerical issue. Cross-coupled flux, positivity, mass conservation and concentrated peaks; spurious undershoots must not be mistaken for physical aggregation or blowup.
Proposed verification. With zero total cell flux check ∫n conservation, homogeneous equilibria and linear growth; refine the peak and domain before discussing singularity. Use manufactured smooth solutions before aggregation cases.
Model convention. This is a common two-field reduction of a more detailed original formulation. Blowup thresholds depend on dimension, domain, boundary and chemical dynamics.
Sources: Keller, Evelyn F. and Segel, Lee A. (1970).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 12 · 1972 · Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#12-1972-gierermeinhardt-activatorinhibitor
Coverage: reading

Pattern formation · Survey only. A representative simplified short-range activation/long-range inhibition model.
a_t=D_a\Delta a+\rho a^2/h-\mu a+\sigma_a,\qquad h_t=D_h\Delta h+\rho_h a^2-\nu h.
Numerical issue. The inhibitor denominator can become singular; positive h, narrow peaks and reaction stiffness require explicit treatment.
Proposed verification. Choose a positive homogeneous equilibrium, check its dispersion relation and inhibitor positivity, then refine spike width and pattern wavelength.
Model convention. Source densities, saturation and baseline production vary across the model family. This simplified formula is not a verbatim transcription of every original variant.
Sources: Gierer, Alfred and Meinhardt, Hans (1972).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 13 · 1972 · Fluid–elastic structure and immersed boundaries# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#13-1972-fluidelastic-structure-and-immersed-boundaries
Coverage: reading

Biomechanics · Survey only. Fluid coupled to a deformable structure; biological examples include valves and membranes, once a force/constitutive law is supplied.
\rho(\boldsymbol u_t+\boldsymbol u\cdot\nabla\boldsymbol u)=-\nabla p+\mu\Delta\boldsymbol u+\boldsymbol f,\quad\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol u=0,\quad\boldsymbol X_t=\boldsymbol u(\boldsymbol X,t).
Numerical issue. Stiff elastic forces, pressure projection, Eulerian–Lagrangian interpolation/spreading and volume leakage.
Proposed verification. Specify elastic energy and force before solving. Check force transfer, adjoint interpolation/spreading, fluid divergence and enclosed-volume drift on a simple relaxing boundary.
Model convention. Immersed boundary is a numerical coupling method, not itself a closed biological constitutive equation. The existing periodic MAC solver does not implement this coupling.
Sources: Peskin, Charles S. (1972).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 14 · 1977 · Chemical master equation and Gillespie SSA# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#14-1977-chemical-master-equation-and-gillespie-ssa
Coverage: reading

Separate fixed-input example: Immigration–death SSA: exact transient laws. Integer molecule counts, reaction jumps νj and propensities aj; SSA samples paths of this continuous-time Markov model.
\partial_t P(\boldsymbol n,t)=\sum_j\left[a_j(\boldsymbol n-\boldsymbol\nu_j)P(\boldsymbol n-\boldsymbol\nu_j,t)-a_j(\boldsymbol n)P(\boldsymbol n,t)\right].
Numerical issue. Correct combinatorial propensities, event ordering, absorbing states and statistical error; tau-leaping is a separate approximation.
Proposed verification. Use immigration–death reactions ∅→X at constant rate k and X→∅ at rate γn: stationary counts are Poisson(k/γ). Compare ensemble mean, variance and distribution with confidence intervals.
Model convention. The 1977 paper is a foundational SSA reference, not a priority claim for all master equations. SSA is a solver; the reaction network is the model. A seed documents a trajectory, not an ensemble validation.
Sources: Gillespie, Daniel T. (1977).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 15 · 1977 · Mackey–Glass delayed physiological feedback# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#15-1977-mackeyglass-delayed-physiological-feedback
Coverage: reading

Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Delayed feedback in a normalized physiological control model; delay can change stability and oscillatory behavior.
\dot x(t)=\frac{\beta x(t-\tau)}{1+x(t-\tau)^p}-\gamma x(t).
Numerical issue. A history function over [−τ,0], delayed interpolation, propagated derivative discontinuities and delay-aware adaptive stepping.
Proposed verification. Check the τ=0 ODE limit, a constant equilibrium history and a manufactured forced solution. Compare long-time statistics rather than expecting chaotic trajectories to match pointwise indefinitely.
Model convention. A scalar initial value alone is insufficient. The delayed ODE is distinct from a spatial reaction–diffusion model.
Sources: Mackey, Michael C. and Glass, Leon (1977).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 16 · 1978 · Replicator evolutionary game dynamics# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#16-1978-replicator-evolutionary-game-dynamics
Coverage: reading

Evolutionary dynamics · Survey only. Strategy fractions reproduce according to relative payoff in a specified matrix game.
\dot x_i=x_i[(A\boldsymbol x)_i-\boldsymbol x^TA\boldsymbol x],\qquad x_i\geq0,\quad\sum_i x_i=1.
Numerical issue. Preserving the probability simplex, behavior near extinction boundaries, neutral cycles versus attracting equilibria.
Proposed verification. Check simplex conservation, exact invariant faces and an analytically chosen game equilibrium; use the appropriate game-specific invariant or Lyapunov function.
Model convention. No universal Lyapunov function or equivalence of fixed point and evolutionarily stable strategy is assumed.
Sources: Taylor, Peter D. and Jonker, Leo B. (1978).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 17 · 1979 · Schnakenberg reaction–diffusion# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#17-1979-schnakenberg-reactiondiffusion
Coverage: reading

Finite-amplitude nonlinear evolution and post-growth patterns compared with independent references and separate space/time refinement; no general pattern-selection claim. A simple autocatalytic kinetic law extended in space, useful for reproducible Turing-onset tests.
u_t=D_u\Delta u+a-u+u^2v,\qquad v_t=D_v\Delta v+b-u^2v.
Numerical issue. Reaction stiffness, positive concentrations and the distinction between kinetic Hopf and spatial Turing instabilities.
Proposed verification. Check u*=a+b, v*=b/(a+b)², then compare mode-growth rates with the linearized discrete and continuum operators under fixed boundaries.
Model convention. A mathematical chemical pattern model; matching a visual biological pattern does not calibrate it to a tissue.
Sources: Schnakenberg, Jürgen (1979).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 18 · 1979 · Shigesada–Kawasaki–Teramoto cross-diffusion# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#18-1979-shigesadakawasakiteramoto-cross-diffusion
Coverage: reading

Population and ecology · Survey only. Competition with density-dependent self- and cross-dispersal can produce spatial segregation.
u_t=\Delta[(d_1+\alpha_{11}u+\alpha_{12}v)u]+u(a_1-b_1u-c_1v),\quad v_t=\Delta[(d_2+\alpha_{21}u+\alpha_{22}v)v]+v(a_2-b_2u-c_2v).
Numerical issue. A coupled nonlinear diffusion matrix, loss of simple scalar maximum-principle arguments, positivity and entropy-compatible discretization.
Proposed verification. Start with manufactured smooth solutions and constant-state equilibria. With reactions removed and no normal flux, conserve each species mass; check coefficient assumptions before claiming an entropy law.
Model convention. The displayed homogeneous-environment reduction omits the original environmental-potential terms. It is not equivalent to two independent scalar diffusion equations.
Sources: Shigesada, Nanako and Kawasaki, Kohkichi and Teramoto, Ei (1979).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 19 · 1983 · Gray–Scott spatial autocatalysis# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#19-1983-grayscott-spatial-autocatalysis
Coverage: reading

Pattern formation · Survey only. A chemical feed/decay model whose spatial extension supports diverse spot and wave patterns.
u_t=D_u\Delta u-uv^2+F(1-u),\qquad v_t=D_v\Delta v+uv^2-(F+k)v.
Numerical issue. Sensitivity to F,k, diffusion, domain and finite-amplitude initial perturbations; grid-scale patterns and floating-point variation can affect long-time morphology.
Proposed verification. Record every parameter and the perturbation seed. Verify the homogeneous (1,0) state and early perturbation response, then perform grid/time refinement of quantitative observables.
Model convention. 1983 is the well-mixed CSTR source; Pearson 1993 is the spatial pattern reference. Spot division does not by itself demonstrate cell division or a linear Turing instability.
Sources: Gray, Peter and Scott, Stephen K. (1983), Pearson, John E. (1993).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 20 · 1996 · Aliev–Panfilov cardiac excitation# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#20-1996-alievpanfilov-cardiac-excitation
Coverage: reading

Excitable systems · Survey only. A reduced phenomenological excitation/recovery model for cardiac waves and restitution.
u_t=D\Delta u-ku(u-a)(u-1)-uv,\quad v_t=\left(\epsilon_0+\frac{\mu_1v}{u+\mu_2}\right)[-v-ku(u-b-1)].
Numerical issue. Stiff recovery, denominator behavior and sensitivity of wave speed/restitution to resolution and time splitting.
Proposed verification. Select a specific model encoding and parameters; establish single-cell and 1D conduction convergence before 2D reentry. Compare a restitution curve, not only a spiral image.
Model convention. Monodomain/bidomain tissue models add conductivity tensors and, for bidomain, an extracellular elliptic constraint. They are not automatically included by this two-variable model.
Sources: Aliev, R. R. and Panfilov, A. V. (1996).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 21 · 2000 · Repressilator mRNA–protein network# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#21-2000-repressilator-mrnaprotein-network
Coverage: reading

Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Three repressing genes form a cyclic network; retaining mRNA and protein gives six state variables.
\dot m_i=\frac{\alpha}{1+p_{i-1}^n}+\alpha_0-m_i,\quad\dot p_i=\beta(m_i-p_i),\qquad i=1,2,3\ \text{cyclic}.
Numerical issue. Multiple degradation scales, oscillation onset, phase error and differences between deterministic cycles and noisy individual-cell behavior.
Proposed verification. Check the symmetric equilibrium and its linear stability. Compare period and amplitude under time refinement after a stated transient.
Model convention. The six-variable form is distinct from a reduced three-protein oscillator; oscillations are parameter-dependent.
Sources: Elowitz, Michael B. and Leibler, Stanislas (2000).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — 22 · 2000 · Genetic toggle switch# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#22-2000-genetic-toggle-switch
Coverage: reading

Delay and gene regulation · Survey only. Mutual repression produces a possible bistable genetic switch in a normalized model.
\dot u=\frac{\alpha_1}{1+v^p}-u,\qquad\dot v=\frac{\alpha_2}{1+u^q}-v.
Numerical issue. Parameter-dependent bistability, saddle separatrices, continuation and sensitivity to perturbations near basin boundaries.
Proposed verification. Find all positive equilibria and their Jacobian eigenvalues; verify hysteresis with sufficiently slow continuation and multiple initial conditions.
Model convention. Bistability is not guaranteed for arbitrary Hill exponents or production rates. Induction, mRNA dynamics and noise are additional model choices.
Sources: Gardner, Timothy S. and Cantor, Charles R. and Collins, James J. (2000).

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — A verification path before attractive movies# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#a-verification-path-before-attractive-movies
Coverage: reading

A practical first sequence is logistic/SIR → full enzyme kinetics →
Fisher front → FitzHugh–Nagumo pulse → Schnakenberg modes → Keller–Segel
aggregation. Predator–prey can run alongside the Hamiltonian notebook as a
long-time invariant test, while a birth–death SSA provides the first stochastic
branch. Gray–Scott is a later visually useful chemical exhibit, with explicit
feed rates, spatial scales, initial perturbation and source attribution.
This order is an implementation proposal, separate from the historical order.

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — An exact nonlinear front# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#an-exact-nonlinear-front
Coverage: reading

For the scaled Fisher equation, the special front of
Ablowitz–Zeppetella (1979) gives a
particularly useful deterministic reference:
u(x,t)=\left[1+\exp\left(\sqrt{\frac r{6D}}(x-ct-x_0)\right)\right]^{-2},
\qquad c=5\sqrt{\frac{Dr}{6}}.
A finite interval should use matching time-dependent analytic boundary data,
or put boundaries far enough away and quantify the truncation effect. Compare
front location, profile norms and temporal/spatial refinement separately.
The special explicit front travels faster than the minimal-speed front;
confusing these two reference problems would produce a false solver error.

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — Pattern onset is a quantitative test# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#pattern-onset-is-a-quantitative-test
Coverage: reading

For a chosen two-species reaction equilibrium, form its Jacobian J. On the
continuum, a Fourier mode with wavevector k evolves under
L(k)=J-|k|^2\operatorname{diag}(D_u,D_v).
On a uniform square grid with a centered Laplacian, replace |k|² by
\kappa_h^2=\frac4{h^2}
\left[\sin^2(k_xh/2)+\sin^2(k_yh/2)\right].
Seed one small eigenmode, measure its early exponential growth and compare
both dispersion relations. A stable k=0 reaction system and an unstable
nonzero mode diagnose the selected diffusion-driven instability; nonlinear
late-time spots alone do not. Schnakenberg supplies a simple kinetic law for
this exercise; it should not be silently substituted for Turing's own example.
Periodic and zero-flux boundaries admit different mode sets.

## Biological model equations and numerical verification — Preserve the model before judging the method# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/biological-models/#preserve-the-model-before-judging-the-method
Coverage: reading

Each future run should specify dimensional or normalized variables, the full
parameter set, boundary/initial conditions, units, random seed where relevant,
model version and source. Balances include boundary flux and source terms:
not every biological reaction–diffusion problem conserves each species mass.
Positivity fixes that clip values may change totals and extinction thresholds.
An implicit diffusion step alone does not prove positivity of a split update.
For stochastic networks, distinguish discretization/model approximation from
finite-ensemble sampling uncertainty. For nonlinear reaction networks the ODE
solution need not equal the exact stochastic mean. For delayed equations,
record the history function and interpolation rule. For biochemical reductions,
measure the model-reduction error separately from integration error.

Murray's third-edition introduction (2002)
provides a broad reading route across these branches. Physiome's
Hodgkin–Huxley workspace

are model-version references to inspect before choosing implementation

Separate follow-up surveys could cover neural population fields, spatial
stochastic reaction–diffusion, intracellular polarity and mass-conserving
reaction networks, cell-cycle size structure, vertex/phase-field cell
mechanics, tumor/nutrient free boundaries, and population genetics with drift.
These are additional branches, not a claim that the current 22 entries exhaust
biological modeling. Numerical verification against a stated equation is also
different from validation against organism- or experiment-specific data.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/
Coverage: reading

A forward problem computes a state from a coefficient; an inverse problem estimates that coefficient from observations of the state. Fit one Bratu parameter λ to five observations and use the previous chapter’s discrete adjoint gradient in the actual optimization updates. The model, boundary conditions and observation positions are known in this small synthetic problem.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Specify the known inputs and the unknown parameter [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#inverse-data
Coverage: reading

State u, coordinate x and coefficient λ are dimensionless in this educational model. The grid, interval [0,1], zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, observation operator H and weights W are fixed. Only λ is unknown; model form and boundary values are not inferred simultaneously. Use centered differences with n interior unknowns and re-solve the nonlinear equation at each trial parameter.
-u^{\prime\prime}-\lambda e^u=0,\quad u(0)=u(1)=0,\qquad F_h(u,\lambda)=D_hu-\lambda e^u=0,\quad D_h=h^{-2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1),\quad h=(n+1)^{-1}.u_\alpha(x)=-2\log\!\frac{\cosh(\alpha(x-1/2))}{\cosh(\alpha/2)},\quad\lambda(\alpha)=\frac{2\alpha^2}{\cosh^2(\alpha/2)},\qquad\alpha_*=1.5,\quad\lambda_*\approx2.684636137266.
The generating values are α*=1.5 and λ*≈2.684636137266. Restrict λ to [0.2,3.4] and start every state solve at zero to target the smaller-solution branch. Numerical branch selection is part of the problem specification. Fitting on the upper branch or continuing through a fold is not verified.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Observation operators and weighted least squares [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#least-squares
Coverage: reading

x_{\rm obs}=(1/8,1/4,1/2,3/4,7/8),\qquad r_h(\lambda)=H_hu_h(\lambda)-d,\quad W=\operatorname{diag}(w_j),\quad w_j=1/5.
Five sensors lie at x=0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.875. They coincide with grid nodes for n=15,31,63,127, so H selects interior state entries; no interpolation error is introduced. A row observing a fixed zero endpoint is zero. Save the observations d before optimization and keep them fixed rather than regenerating them for each trial λ.
\Phi_h(\lambda)=\frac12 r_h(\lambda)^TWr_h(\lambda)+\frac\gamma2(\lambda-\lambda_{\rm prior})^2,\qquad\gamma\ge0,\quad\ell=0.2\le\lambda\le b=3.4.
All published experiments use γ=0 and wⱼ=1/5, making the objective half the mean squared observation residual. The implementation also accepts positive nonuniform weights and γ≥0, with separate tests for the weights and explicit prior term. Interpreting W as an inverse error covariance would require a specified probability model; none is assumed here.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Build an adjoint gradient from observation residuals [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#adjoint-gradient
Coverage: reading

J=F_u=D_h-\lambda\operatorname{diag}(e^u),\quad F_\lambda=-e^u,\quad q=H_h^TWr_h,\qquad J^Tp=q.\frac{d\Phi_h}{d\lambda}=\underbrace{\gamma(\lambda-\lambda_{\rm prior})}_{\text{explicit parameter term}}-p^TF_\lambda=\gamma(\lambda-\lambda_{\rm prior})+p^Te^u.
The state partial derivative q includes both the transpose of H and the observation weights. With the Lagrangian convention Φ−pᵀF, subtract pᵀF_λ from the explicit parameter derivative. Since F_λ=−exp(u), the Bratu state-mediated term has a plus sign. Setting γ=0 removes the explicit term, not the state-mediated term.
Assemble J at the converged primal state and solve Jᵀp=q using the existing implicit-differentiation linear algebra. Do not differentiate an unrolled Newton iteration sequence. This Bratu J is symmetric: an independent nonsymmetric manufactured problem tests transposition in the previous release, while the new dedicated tests check the observation operator, nonuniform weights and regularization.
There is one parameter and one objective, so a direct sensitivity solve Js=exp(u) also has one right-hand side. This example demonstrates no adjoint speed advantage. It checks a construction that can extend to many parameters on a small inverse problem.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Run a gradient method with box constraints [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#bounded-optimization
Coverage: reading

\Pi_{[\ell,b]}(z)=\min(b,\max(\ell,z)),\qquad\lambda_{\rm trial}=\Pi_{[\ell,b]}(\lambda_k-a g_k),\quad\Delta\lambda=\lambda_{\rm trial}-\lambda_k.\Phi_h(\lambda_{\rm trial})\le\Phi_h(\lambda_k)+c g_k\Delta\lambda,\qquad c=10^{-4},\quad a=10\,2^{-j},\quad j=0,1,\ldots .
Update λ using its current adjoint gradient g and project into the interval. Restart the step length at a=10 on each iteration and halve it until the sufficient-decrease inequality holds. Use the actual displacement after projection in gΔλ. Accepted and rejected trial evaluations use the same primal controls. A failed state solve stops the calculation rather than supplying a valid objective value.
G(\lambda)=\lambda-\Pi_{[\ell,b]}(\lambda-g(\lambda)),\qquad |G(\lambda)|\le10^{-10}.
The stopping measure is the absolute projected-gradient mapping with a unit step. It equals the ordinary gradient at an interior solution where projection is inactive; at an active bound a nonzero g can satisfy constrained stationarity. Save every accepted point, step length, backtrack count, primal/adjoint residual and termination reason, with at most 300 updates and 50 line-search trials. A small objective change alone is not the convergence test.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Run a gradient method with box constraints [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#bounded-optimization
Coverage: reading

Armijo (1966) provides the sufficient-decrease and variable-step idea; this implementation applies it to the projected displacement. The original unconstrained convergence theorem is not cited as a global-convergence guarantee for this nonlinear inverse problem. This is also not an implementation of BFGS or a general constrained-optimization library.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Keep three synthetic data regimes distinct [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#synthetic-data
Coverage: reading

d^{\rm disc}=H_hu_h(\lambda_*),\qquad d^{\rm cont}_j=u_{\alpha_*}(x_j),\qquad d^{\rm noisy}=d^{\rm cont}+10^{-3}(1,-0.6,0.4,-1,0.3)^T.
Noiseless data from the same discretization. Generate d with the n=31 forward solver and invert with that same discretization. Recovering λ* is an inverse crime: it checks consistency among data generation, observations, gradient and optimizer, not accuracy for the continuous problem or real measurements.
Noiseless data from the independent continuous family. Fix the closed-form u_α values at the observation points. Refine the inverse grid through n=15,31,63,127 to examine discretization bias in the difference from the generating parameter.
Data with a fixed perturbation. Add the displayed deterministic vector once to the same continuous observations. No random draw or known noise distribution is assumed, and no resampling occurs. The published perturbed-data fit uses n=63. A best fit displaced from λ* need not indicate optimizer failure.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Verification: gradients, optimization, grids and observations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#inverse-verification
Coverage: reading

The saved measurements and input data record figure values, controls, residuals and termination reasons.
g_{\rm FD}(\varepsilon)=\frac{\Phi_h(\lambda+\varepsilon)-\Phi_h(\lambda-\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon},\qquad F_h(u_h(\lambda\pm\varepsilon),\lambda\pm\varepsilon)=0.
Check gradients away from stationary points. Re-solve the state at λ±ε for several λ and compare objective-only central differences with adjoint gradients. Do not rely only on both gradients being nearly zero at an optimum.
Use an independent scalar reference. Compare the adjoint-gradient fit with objective-only golden-section search. Golden section assumes a unimodal objective; sampled objective landscapes are also saved. Agreement is not a proof of global optimality across all branches.
Use three starting values. Compare accepted updates, objective decrease, projected gradients and termination reasons from 0.5,1.5,3.2.
Vary the data generation and grid separately. Record same-discretization consistency, mesh error for continuous data and the shift in best fit under the fixed perturbation.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Verification: gradients, optimization, grids and observations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#inverse-verification
Coverage: reading

Saved measurements 1: gradient checks. At n=31 and λ=0.8,1.8,3.0, central differences with ε=10⁻⁵ differ from adjoint gradients by approximately 1.31×10⁻¹², 2.81×10⁻¹² and 1.79×10⁻¹². The maximum absolute direct-sensitivity/adjoint gradient difference is below 1.4×10⁻¹⁷. The JSON also saves a perturbation sweep. These check derivatives of the implemented discrete objective.
Measurements 2: same-discretization recovery. For n=31, starts λ=0.5,1.5,3.2 take 33,30,25 accepted updates. Absolute errors from λ* are approximately 1.48×10⁻⁹, 1.10×10⁻⁹ and 1.65×10⁻⁹. All three projected gradients are at most 10⁻¹⁰ and data RMS residuals below 3.9×10⁻¹⁰. Read this close agreement as a same-discretization consistency check.
Measurements 3: mesh dependence for continuous data. For n=15,31,63,127, fitted λ values are approximately 2.6816989071, 2.6839024768, 2.6844527616, 2.6845902950. Absolute errors from λ* are approximately 2.9372×10⁻³, 7.3366×10⁻⁴, 1.8338×10⁻⁴, 4.5842×10⁻⁵, decreasing by about four as h halves. Observed orders are 2.0013, 2.0003, 2.0001. The optimizer converges while finite-mesh bias remains.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Verification: gradients, optimization, grids and observations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#inverse-verification
Coverage: reading

Measurements 4: a fixed perturbation shifts the best fit. At n=63 the fitted λ≈2.6841620622 shifts by about −2.9070×10⁻⁴ from the unperturbed optimum on the same grid. Absolute error from λ* is about 4.7408×10⁻⁴, data RMS residual about 7.1942×10⁻⁴ and objective about 2.5878×10⁻⁷. The projected gradient is about 6.39×10⁻¹¹, so the departure from truth is not explained simply by unfinished optimization.
The four continuous-data fits and the fixed-perturbation fit agree with the objective-only golden-section reference to within 2.1×10⁻⁹ in λ. The reference’s final interval width is below about 8.65×10⁻⁹; it is not a certificate of an exact optimum. Primal residuals at the eight final fits above are at most 1.4×10⁻¹¹. ## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Observations that can and cannot identify λ [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#identifiability
Coverage: reading

J s=e^u,\qquad \frac{d(H_hu_h)}{d\lambda}=H_hs,\qquad \|W^{1/2}H_hs\|_2>0\ \text{is a local sensitivity diagnostic}.
A response of the interior observations to λ is a useful local sensitivity diagnostic in this scalar problem. A weak response can amplify small data changes into large parameter changes. Local sensitivity alone does not prove global uniqueness. Changing the branch, sensor positions or admissible interval changes the inverse problem.
For a counterexample, observe only x=0,1. Their fixed Dirichlet values vanish independently of λ, so H=0 and Hs=0. With γ=0, the objective is independent of λ and the data cannot identify it. Dedicated tests check this property, and the fitting function rejects this setting as uninformative. A regularization term could select a parameter but would not make the boundary observations informative.
The fixed-perturbation experiment supplies no statistical confidence intervals. Real observations, unknown model discrepancy, optimal sensor placement and identifiability of many parameters are outside the verified scope.

## Bratu inverse problem: estimate λ from synthetic observations with adjoint gradients — Separate parameter error from optimization error [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-inverse/#error-scope
Coverage: reading

e_\lambda=|\widehat\lambda_h-\lambda_*|,\qquad r_{\rm data}=\sqrt{\frac15\sum_{j=1}^5(H_hu_h-d)_j^2},\qquad r_F=\|F_h(u_h,\lambda)\|_2,\quad r_p=\|J^Tp-q\|_2.
Error from the generating λ*, observation residual, primal residual, adjoint residual and projected gradient are different quantities. A small projected gradient checks stationarity for the chosen grid, observations and constraints; it does not guarantee truth recovery or a zero observation residual. Conversely, continuous/discrete mismatch or fixed observation perturbations can move a well-converged optimum away from λ*.
Primal solves use an unscaled Euclidean residual tolerance of 10⁻¹⁰ and at most 40 updates. Adjoint systems use small dense matrices. Finite-difference gradient checks balance perturbation truncation, roundoff and inner-solve error. Mesh refinement, tighter optimizer stopping and improvement of a physical model address different errors.
This release is an educational scalar, box-constrained fit on a specified Bratu branch. It is not a general inverse-problem library, quasi-Newton implementation, transient adjoint, singular-point continuation method, model-selection procedure or validation of a physical model with experimental data.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Extend constant λ to a level and a slope [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#multi-parameter-model
Coverage: reading

-u^{\prime\prime}(x)-\lambda(x;\theta)e^{u(x)}=0,\quad u(0)=u(1)=0,\quad \lambda(x;\theta)=a+b(2x-1),\quad\theta=(a,b)^T.\mathcal B=[1,2.8]\times[-0.5,0.5],\qquad 0.5\le\lambda(x;\theta)\le3.3,\qquad \theta_*=(2.2,0.35)^T.F_h(u,\theta)=D_hu-(Q_h\theta)\odot e^u=0,\quad (Q_h)_{i,:}=(1,2x_i-1),\quad D_h=h^{-2}\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1).
The unknown a sets the coefficient level and b multiplies the tilt basis (2x−1). The actual spatial derivative dλ/dx and the end-to-end difference λ(1)−λ(0) both equal 2b. Setting b=0 recovers the constant-coefficient Bratu model. This is a two-basis-function extension of the coefficient, rather than duplicate estimates of one constant λ. State, coordinate and both parameters are dimensionless. Domain, mesh, zero Dirichlet data and observation operator are fixed.
The published experiments use the box and generating vector θ*=(2.2,0.35) above. A positive coefficient does not imply identifiability. These bounds alone do not guarantee existence, uniqueness or convergence for arbitrary meshes and starting states. Every primal solve starts at zero and uses damped Newton with an explicit residual acceptance check; the tested smaller-solution branch defines the scope.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Fix the observations and their numerical generator [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#observations-and-data
Coverage: reading

The ordinary experiment samples x=0.125,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.875. All are exact interior nodes on the inverse meshes, so H selects state components. Observations at mirrored locations are retained separately: symmetric sensor positions do not discard the left-right difference. The published weights are wⱼ=1/5. They weight observations, rather than approximate a spatial integral.
A noiseless control generated and fitted on the same mesh first checks recovery of both coefficients. It is an inverse crime used for code consistency. Separate fixed observations from a numerical reference, with its own refinement check, support inverse-mesh refinement. For b≠0 we do not reuse the closed-form constant-coefficient Bratu family as an analytic reference. The saved inputs and evidence specify the actual generator, resolution and self-refinement difference.
The numerical generator uses a separate Newton implementation with Thomas elimination for tridiagonal systems. Grids n=255,511,1023 are compared, and n=1023 observations are fixed. Linear-system implementations differ, but both use second-order centered finite differences. The finer grid is not an exact continuous solution, and parameter error also contains its finite-grid error. Generator controls use the infinity norm of h²F and final Newton correction, recorded separately from the unscaled inverse-solve residual.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Obtain both gradient components from one adjoint equation [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#multi-adjoint-gradient
Coverage: reading

r_h(\theta)=H_hu_h(\theta)-d,\qquad\Phi_\gamma(\theta)=\underbrace{\tfrac12r_h^TWr_h}_{\Phi_{\rm data}}+\underbrace{\tfrac\gamma2\|\theta-\theta_{\rm prior}\|_2^2}_{\Phi_{\rm prior}},\quad\gamma\ge0.J=F_u=D_h-\operatorname{diag}\!\big((Q_h\theta)\odot e^u\big),\qquad B_\theta=F_\theta=-\operatorname{diag}(e^u)Q_h.q=H_h^TWr_h,\qquad J^Tp=q,\qquad g=\nabla_\theta\Phi_\gamma=\gamma(\theta-\theta_{\rm prior})-B_\theta^Tp=\gamma(\theta-\theta_{\rm prior})+Q_h^T(e^u\odot p).
Assume a smooth selected state branch and a locally nonsingular state Jacobian J. Invertibility of the primal Jacobian J and full column rank of the observation Jacobian Adata are separate conditions. With the Lagrangian convention Φ−pᵀF, the residual parameter derivative Bθ has two columns, while p has one right-hand side. The state partial q includes Hᵀ and W. Multiplication by Bθᵀp produces both components of g. The state-mediated term Qᵀ(exp(u)⊙p) remains when γ=0. We differentiate the converged discrete equation, rather than unroll a finite sequence of Newton iterations.
JS=-B_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(e^u)Q_h,\qquad S=\frac{\partial u_h}{\partial\theta}\in\mathbb R^{n\times2}.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Obtain both gradient components from one adjoint equation [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#multi-adjoint-gradient
Coverage: reading

The direct sensitivity S uses two right-hand sides. It provides an independent gradient diagnostic. Actual optimization directions use the adjoint gradient; neither finite differences nor direct sensitivities substitute for it. A two-parameter example with small dense matrices does not establish an unmeasured speed advantage.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Vary regularization and inspect prior bias [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#regularization
Coverage: reading

The Tikhonov-type quadratic penalty adds distance from θprior to the observation misfit. The implementation uses Euclidean distance, equivalent to the regularization matrix R=I₂. Zero, weak and stronger penalties are applied to identical observations, recording data residual, distance from the prior and error against the generating vector separately. Increasing γ need not move the estimate closer to the generating truth.
A displaced prior pulls the estimate toward its own values. Regularization may suppress amplification of observation perturbations along a weak direction while introducing prior bias. A synthetic experiment can compare parameter errors because θ* is known; this does not supply a corresponding choice rule for real data. The published γ sweep illustrates sensitivity and bias. It does not validate automatic tuning, cross-validation, an L-curve corner rule or statistical confidence intervals.
Hansen’s author-maintained manual describes the quadratic penalty, augmented least squares and spectral analysis. Its squared regularization parameter corresponds to γ here. Its linear formulas are distinguished from this implemented nonlinear coefficient fit.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Optimize with a fixed scaling of the adjoint gradient [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#bounded-fit
Coverage: reading

\theta_{\rm trial}=\Pi_{\mathcal B}(\theta_k-sP g_k),\quad\Delta\theta=\theta_{\rm trial}-\theta_k,\qquad\Phi_\gamma(\theta_{\rm trial})\le\Phi_\gamma(\theta_k)+c\,g_k^T\Delta\theta,\quad P=\operatorname{diag}(1,100),\ s=10\,2^{-j},\ c=10^{-4}.G(\theta)=\theta-\Pi_{\mathcal B}(\theta-g(\theta)),\qquad\|G(\theta)\|_\infty\le10^{-9}.
P=diag(1,100) is a fixed positive diagonal matrix that adjusts progress along the differently sensitive level and slope directions. The evidence records P, initial step, halving rule, Armijo constant, iteration limits and tolerances. P adds no observation and is not a Gauss–Newton matrix estimated from the data. Rescaling an optimizer is distinct from improving identifiability.
The Armijo inner product uses the actual projected displacement Δθ. Stopping uses the unit-step projected gradient G without P, so a small preconditioned update alone cannot imply convergence. A bound-constrained stationary point may have nonzero gradient components at active bounds. At most 1000 updates and 50 backtracking trials are allowed. Inspect the termination reason and accepted history; closeness to the generating vector is not a stopping criterion.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Diagnose data-only sensitivity with singular values [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#data-identifiability
Coverage: reading

A_{\rm data}=W^{1/2}H_hS\in\mathbb R^{m\times2},\quad A_{\rm data}=U\Sigma V^T,\quad\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge0,\qquad\|A_{\rm data}v_2\|_2=\sigma_2.\Delta\theta=T\Delta z,\quad A_z=A_{\rm data}T,\qquad\delta(W^{1/2}Hu)\approx A_{\rm data}\Delta\theta=A_z\Delta z.
Adata linearizes changes in weighted observations as the parameters change. The right singular vector v₂ associated with a small σ₂ identifies a coefficient combination with little effect on those observations. Two independent observed directions yield full column rank at this point. This is a local diagnostic for the chosen state branch and observation operator, rather than a proof of global uniqueness for the nonlinear inverse problem.
Singular values and condition numbers depend on observation weights, parameter units and parameter scaling. The published SVD uses T=I₂, the raw (a,b) coordinates. Changes of units or coefficient basis require the scaling to be stated. Numerical rank counts singular values above 10⁻¹⁰σ₁ and records that absolute threshold as well. A small singular value is not a universal identification threshold independent of measurement precision and floating-point error.
A_{\rm aug}=\begin{pmatrix}A_{\rm data}\\ \sqrt\gamma I_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad A_{\rm aug}^TA_{\rm aug}=A_{\rm data}^TA_{\rm data}+\gamma I_2.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Diagnose data-only sensitivity with singular values [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#data-identifiability
Coverage: reading

Positive γ raises the singular-value floor of this local augmented matrix. The term γI₂ comes from a prior penalty, not new observations. AdataᵀAdata+γI₂ is a regularized Gauss–Newton-type local curvature; it is not generally the exact Hessian at nonzero residual, nor proof of global convexity. Data-only and augmented diagnostics are separate in the evidence.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Exhibit information lost by a central observation [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#reflection-ambiguity
Coverage: reading

u_h(a,-b;x_i)=u_h(a,b;1-x_i),\qquad u_h(a,-b;1/2)=u_h(a,b;1/2).H_{\rm center}S\in\mathbb R^{1\times2}\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{rank}(H_{\rm center}S)\le1;\qquad \left.\frac{\partial u_h(1/2)}{\partial b}\right|_{b=0}=0.
A single observation at x=1/2 gives a 1×2 observation Jacobian, whose rank is at most one at every θ. At b=0 the state is even about the center and the slope sensitivity is odd, so the center has zero first derivative with respect to b. Moreover, reflection x↦1−x changes b to −b while preserving the central value. Opposite slope signs are observationally indistinguishable there. This is information lost by H, not a floating-point defect or merely stalled optimization.
Fits using center-only data and mirrored priors check that regularized estimates depend on prior choice. Obtaining a smooth stationary point or a positive regularized local curvature does not show that the data identified the slope sign. A penalty may select a solution by adding an assumption; it does not create the missing observational information.

A compact SVD of a 1×2 matrix returns only one singular value. Its lack of a second returned entry must not be read as absence of a null direction. We retain the zero direction and right singular vectors in the full two-dimensional parameter space. Five sensors and one central sensor are compared through independent sensitivities, not their counts alone.

Fixed reference observations and meshes. Refine the inverse mesh while keeping the numerical reference data fixed. Report reference-generation error checks; this is not an error against an exact continuous solution.
One perturbation and a γ sweep. Hold observations and prior fixed while comparing fit residual, distance from the prior and parameter error.

## Multi-parameter Bratu inversion: regularization and identifiability — Distinguish why an estimate moves and what was verified [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/bratu-multi-inverse/#error-and-scope

e_\theta=\|\widehat\theta-\theta_*\|_2,\quad\rho_d=\|W^{1/2}r_h\|_2,\quad\rho_F=\|F_h\|_2,\quad\rho_p=\|J^Tp-q\|_2.\qquad \rho_d\ne\rho_F.
Generating-parameter error, observation fit, primal residual, adjoint residual and projected gradient measure different things. Regularization, fixed observation perturbations, inverse discretization and reference-generation errors can shift a fully converged fit away from θ*. Conversely, a small data residual does not establish that both parameters were identified.
Scope is a small dense-matrix example with two fixed coefficient basis functions, box bounds, the smaller-solution branch, known boundary conditions and observation operator, and synthetic data. General function recovery for λ(x), guarantees for many coefficients, BFGS or Gauss–Newton optimization, real measurements, unknown boundaries or model discrepancy, optimal experimental design and probabilistic uncertainty or confidence intervals are outside the checks.

## The carbuncle phenomenon — The carbuncle phenomenon [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/carbuncle/
Coverage: reading

A strong shock can develop a spurious bulge, streaks, or alternating transverse states when captured by a multidimensional numerical scheme. This carbuncle instability is a property of the discretized flow problem; a sharp-looking shock alone does not establish accuracy. Grid-aligned shocks are a particularly revealing setting.
THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data
Quirk (1994) documents failures of Godunov-type solvers and motivates switching between complementary fluxes. Pandolfi and D’Ambrosio (2001) analyze shock-related instabilities and localized remedies. Their analyses motivate the diagnostic questions below; this chapter does not claim a universal mechanism or a new stability proof.

## The carbuncle phenomenon — Why a one-dimensional flux can fail in two dimensions# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/carbuncle/#why-a-one-dimensional-flux-can-fail-in-two-dimensions
Coverage: reading

A face-normal Roe flux has the form
\widehat F_n=\tfrac12(F_n(U_L)+F_n(U_R))
-\tfrac12\sum_k |\widetilde\lambda_k|\,\alpha_k\widetilde r_k.
Its characteristic decomposition gives different dissipation to acoustic, contact, and shear waves. Near a stationary, grid-aligned shock, disturbances in neighboring rows can interact with weakly damped transverse modes and the discrete shock structure. Resolving contacts accurately and stabilizing every strong multidimensional shock are separate design demands. The entire scheme matters: reconstruction, flux, time integration, mesh, and boundaries.
Odd–even decoupling describes alternating neighboring-row behavior and is a useful shock-instability diagnostic. It is related to carbuncle studies, but the terms do not identify one identical test in every paper. The familiar blunt-body shock bulge and a perturbed planar-shock experiment have different geometries and boundary conditions.

## The carbuncle phenomenon — Three different questions# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/carbuncle/#three-different-questions
Coverage: reading

Entropy correction: a transonic rarefaction can be represented by an inadmissible expansion shock. Smoothing a small acoustic eigenvalue addresses this sonic-wave issue. It does not by itself certify multidimensional strong-shock stability.
Positivity: density and pressure must remain admissible. Wave-speed bounds, a suitable CFL restriction, and positivity-preserving reconstruction address this question. Positive states can still contain a carbuncle.
Transverse shock robustness: perturbations along the shock must not grow into a grid-dependent artifact. This requires its own multidimensional evidence.
The library’s 1D Roe entropy smoothing belongs to the first category. Passing Sod or the double-rarefaction test does not answer the third.

## The carbuncle phenomenon — Remedies and their tradeoffs# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/carbuncle/#remedies-and-their-tradeoffs
Coverage: reading

A two-wave HLL/HLLE flux or Rusanov flux usually adds more dissipation to contact and shear information than a contact-resolving solver. A shock sensor can blend a sharper flux with a more dissipative one locally. Rotated or multidimensional flux constructions seek dissipation in directions that a strictly face-normal treatment can miss. See Nishikawa and Kitamura (2008) for a rotated-hybrid approach.
These are design directions, not interchangeable guarantees. A sensor may also damp a physical shear layer; excessive dissipation can conceal an instability while losing the feature of interest. State the actual wave-speed estimate: this atlas’s 2D baseline uses HLL with Davis-type bounds, not an implementation of every Einfeldt HLLE variant.

## The carbuncle phenomenon — What an honest comparison must measure# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/carbuncle/#what-an-honest-comparison-must-measure
Coverage: reading

Use a perturbed planar strong shock, then a blunt-body flow on a controlled grid sequence. Fix the shock Mach number, shock location relative to cell faces, perturbation amplitude and wavelength, boundary conditions, reconstruction, CFL, and final time. Compare Roe, HLL/HLLE, and a proposed hybrid under matched settings. Repeat with shifted or rotated meshes.
For periodic transverse rows, one possible alternating-density diagnostic at a selected shock-normal station is
A_\pi(i,t)=\left|\frac{1}{N_y}\sum_{j=0}^{N_y-1}(-1)^j
\bigl(\rho_{i,j}(t)-\overline\rho_i(t)\bigr)\right|.
Record its time history and the maximum over the shock neighborhood, together with shock position, transverse velocity, pressure, and positivity. For a moving shock, track the shock neighborhood rather than a single fixed column. Other wavelengths need their own diagnostics. A small final residual or a visually smooth contour is insufficient evidence.

## The carbuncle phenomenon — Status in this edition# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/carbuncle/#status-in-this-edition
Coverage: reading

The Double Mach Reflection exhibit is an actual first-order HLL computation of an oblique shock interaction. It is not a controlled Roe-versus-HLL carbuncle experiment and supplies no carbuncle-free certification. The planar-shock section below adds a controlled row-perturbation diagnostic; a separate stage adds conforming-grid cylinder-forebody snapshots and controls. The physical cylindrical viscous stress and numerical shock dissipation also represent different operators.
Continue with Roe’s legacy, the flux benchmarks, and the implementation roadmap.

## The carbuncle phenomenon — Computed planar odd–even diagnostic# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/carbuncle/#computed-planar-oddeven-diagnostic
Coverage: reading

Open the controlled comparison. This independent test
uses a stationary Mach-6 normal shock in [0,1] × [0,0.25], γ=1.4,
upstream (ρ,u,v,p)=(1.4,6,0,1), and exact normal-shock downstream states.
Both x boundaries are fixed, y is periodic, and cells are square. Compare
64 × 16 and 128 × 32 at t=0.2 using first-order space, SSPRK2 and CFL 0.3.
The shock is either at x=0.5, aligned with a face, or half a cell farther right.
Initial conservative means integrate a row-dependent front displacement of
±10⁻⁴Δx exactly. Each configuration has an unperturbed control.
Compare raw Roe, Roe with acoustic smoothing δ=0.1c̃, Davis HLL,
Einfeldt-type HLLE, a pressure-sensor Roe/HLLE blend, and the common-sound-speed
cubic-pressure AUSM baseline. All runs use the same
spatial/time settings; their step counts and costs need not match.
The blend uses S=max_neighbors |p_neighbor−p|/min(p_neighbor,p),
θ=clip((S−0.05)/0.2,0,1), and the maximum adjacent cell θ at each face.
F=(1−θ)F_Roe_fixed+θF_HLLE. The x-pressure jump can therefore activate
HLLE on nearby transverse faces. This is an explicit educational sensor,
not the published rotated-hybrid construction or a universal cure.
Measure max_i Aπ over |x−xshock|<0.1, pressure/density admissibility, retry
counts, transverse velocity and each row's integrated mass-deficit position.

The latter is not a pointwise detected front location. Density maps subtract
the transverse row mean, using one signed color range per comparison.
The history's logarithmic display floors values at 10⁻¹⁶; raw values remain
in the download. No state clipping or hidden flux replacement is used.
Face-aligned Roe runs amplify the chosen row mode; shifting the shock half a
cell changes the response substantially. The entropy correction does not

## Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport — Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chapman-enskog/
Coverage: reading

Chapman–Enskog（チャップマン–エンスコッグ）expansion separates kinetic
relaxation from slowly varying hydrodynamic fields. The classical kinetic
theory is treated by Chapman and Cowling's The Mathematical Theory of
Non-Uniform Gases (first edition 1939; third edition 1970). The book's date
is not the invention date of the expansion. This chapter gives an independent,
unforced, isothermal lattice-BGK derivation at low Mach number.
THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data

## Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport — A small parameter and solvability# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chapman-enskog/#a-small-parameter-and-solvability
Coverage: reading

Introduce a bookkeeping parameter ε for slow variation:
f_q=f_q^{(0)}+\epsilon f_q^{(1)}+\epsilon^2 f_q^{(2)}+\cdots,
\quad \partial_t=\epsilon\partial_{t_1}+\epsilon^2\partial_{t_2},
\quad \nabla=\epsilon\nabla_1.
Conserved moments are carried by the local equilibrium, so higher-order
corrections have zero mass and momentum moments:
\sum_q f_q^{(k)}=0,\quad
\sum_q\boldsymbol c_q f_q^{(k)}=0\quad (k\geq1).
These are constraints on the expansion, not instructions to erase the
nonequilibrium stress. The stress moment of f^(1) produces viscous transport.

## Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport — Keep the discrete-time Taylor term# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chapman-enskog/#keep-the-discrete-time-taylor-term
Coverage: reading

For lattice BGK, expand the streaming side with D_q=∂t+c_q·∇. In lattice
time units the Taylor series starts as D_q f_q + D_q² f_q/2.
At successive orders,
f_q^{(0)}=f_q^{eq},\qquad
f_q^{(1)}=-\tau D_{1q} f_q^{eq},
\partial_{t_2} f_q^{eq}
+\left(1-\frac1{2\tau}\right)D_{1q}f_q^{(1)}
=-\frac{f_q^{(2)}}{\tau}.
The first-order mass and momentum moments give the continuity and Euler
parts. The second-order stress correction supplies the Newtonian viscous
part. D2Q9 equilibrium isotropy, the low-Mach approximation, and the preceding
factor give the shear viscosity
\nu=c_s^2\left(\tau-\frac12\right)\Delta t.
Here τ is the dimensionless number of lattice time steps used for
relaxation, with physical τ_relax=τΔt. Continuous-time BGK instead gives
ν=c_s²τ_relax for the corresponding isothermal model; there is no streaming
Taylor half-step in that continuous equation. Mixing those definitions yields
a wrong viscosity.

## Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport — What this derivation does and does not establish# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chapman-enskog/#what-this-derivation-does-and-does-not-establish
Coverage: reading

The D2Q9 experiment measures shear damping rather than
only substituting this formula. Qian et al. (1992)
is the lattice-model source; the BGK source
concerns continuous kinetic relaxation. Guo et al. (2002)
treats the force discretization separately; the unforced algebra above does
not derive its source term.
This is a formal near-equilibrium asymptotic expansion, with small gradients
and small Mach number for the truncated isothermal equilibrium. It does not
prove stability near shocks, justify arbitrary relaxation times, recover an
energy equation, or make this model a general rarefied-gas Boltzmann solver.
Burnett-order transport and thermal collision models require additional
moments and analysis.

## Chebyshev approximation — Chebyshev approximation [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chebyshev/
Coverage: reading

Chebyshev approximation uses endpoint-clustered nodes and a connection with trigonometric functions. Interpolation, weighted projection and best uniform approximation are distinct constructions.

## Chebyshev approximation — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chebyshev/#model
Coverage: reading

Set Tₖ(cosθ)=cos(kθ) and approximate f on [−1,1] by ΣaₖTₖ. Lobatto nodes xⱼ=cos(jπ/n) allow interpolation coefficients to be computed by a discrete cosine transform. Orthogonality uses weight (1−x²)⁻¹/², not the unit weight of Legendre polynomials.
T_0(x)=1,\quad T_1(x)=x,\quad T_{k+1}(x)=2xT_k(x)-T_{k-1}(x),\qquad x_j=\cos(j\pi/n).

## Chebyshev approximation — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chebyshev/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Map the physical interval, sample the nodes, compute coefficients and evaluate the series by recurrence. Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature integrates the interpolant; its nodes and exactness properties are not identical to Gaussian quadrature.

## Chebyshev approximation — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/chebyshev/#conditions
Coverage: reading

Analytic functions can give rapid coefficient decay, while jumps cause Gibbs oscillations and finite smoothness slows decay. Differentiation amplifies coefficient errors. A small coefficient tail alone cannot rule out unresolved features between sampling nodes.

Test reproduction of Tₖ, nodal interpolation and approximation of exp(x), then compare convergence for an absolute value or jump. Measure errors off the interpolation grid and verify derivative scaling under interval maps.
