## CIP: carry the value and the gradient — CIP: carry the value and the gradient [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/cip/
Coverage: reading

The original cubic-interpolated pseudo-particle (CIP) idea stores a field and
its spatial derivative, then reconstructs an upwind cubic profile. The broader
family is also called constrained interpolation profile. The
CIP notebook
implements the original polynomial construction for constant-speed periodic
scalar advection. It compares value-only linear interpolation with CIP and
checks diffusion, gradient transport, oscillations, refinement, and conservation.
THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data
Historical references are Takewaki–Nishiguchi–Yabe (1985)
and Yabe–Aoki (1991).
The accessible Saito–Obase–Abe-Ouchi (2020) paper
describes CIP-family value/gradient evolution and a rational variant; its
ice-sheet application and RCIP algorithm are separate from this polynomial example.

## CIP: carry the value and the gradient — Characteristics and an additional unknown# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/cip/#characteristics-and-an-additional-unknown
Coverage: reading

For constant velocity a,
f_t+a f_x=0,\qquad g=f_x,\qquad g_t+a g_x=0.
At a receiving point x_i, trace backward to x_d=x_i−a dt. Interpolate both
f and g from the old upwind interval at that departure point. The evolved g
is an independent state variable; it is not replaced after each step by a
finite difference of the updated f. For N nodes, CIP therefore stores 2N
scalar unknowns, while the linear comparison stores N.
For variable velocity the gradient equation instead includes stretching:
g_t+a g_x=-a_xg.
Source terms, velocity variation, and compressibility require additional
updates and characteristic treatment. A transported tracer f_t+a f_x=0 and
a conserved density f_t+(af)_x=0 also differ when a_x is nonzero. This edition
uses constant a only, where the two PDE forms coincide.

## CIP: carry the value and the gradient — Four endpoint constraints determine a cubic# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/cip/#four-endpoint-constraints-determine-a-cubic
Coverage: reading

On an interval of width h, with normalized coordinate s∈[0,1], the cubic is
P(s)=H_{00}(s)f_L+hH_{10}(s)g_L+H_{01}(s)f_R+hH_{11}(s)g_R,
\begin{aligned}
H_{00}&=2s^3-3s^2+1,&H_{10}&=s^3-2s^2+s,\\
H_{01}&=-2s^3+3s^2,&H_{11}&=s^3-s^2.
\end{aligned}
The endpoint values and physical derivatives are reproduced, and the new
states are f_i=P(s_d) and g_i=P′(s_d)/h. Here P′ differentiates with respect
to s. For positive a, the interval is [x_{i−1},x_i] and s_d=1−a dt/h; for
negative a it is [x_i,x_{i+1}] and s_d=−a dt/h. The implementation restricts
|a|dt/h≤1 to keep the departure point in this adjacent interval. The case
|a|dt/h=1 shifts both arrays by one node exactly.
This is a complete characteristic/remapping update for this constant-speed
problem, rather than a spatial RHS subsequently advanced by an arbitrary RK
method. It belongs beside the RK family, not inside its list
of time-integration tableaus. More general semi-Lagrangian schemes can cross
multiple cells; that capability is outside this adjacent-cell example.

## CIP: carry the value and the gradient — Reproducible scalar tests# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/cip/#reproducible-scalar-tests
Coverage: reading

The domain is periodic [0,1], with N=128 point nodes x_i=i/N. Notebook choices
are a=±1, Courant magnitudes 0.25, 0.6, or 1, and final times 0.25 or 1.
The last step is shortened. Every configuration is solved independently to
its selected final time, without interpolation between saved solutions.
The smooth profile is 1+0.2 sin(2πx). Initial g is either its analytic
derivative or the centered periodic difference. The square pulse is one on
[0.2,0.4) and zero elsewhere. Its initial slopes are either zero or centered
differences. Zero is an explicit convention at a sampled discontinuity, not
an analytic derivative there. Consequently there is no square-pulse exact
gradient error displayed.
The reference f is exact translated point samples. These are not the
cell-average references used in the finite-volume limiter notebook.
Reported L1 means the average absolute point error. Initial-gradient choice
can materially affect sharp features. The basic cubic has no TVD, monotonicity,
or positivity limiter, and the square test shows overshoot and undershoot.
The linear interpolation comparison is the same signed-characteristic
point-value update, algebraically first-order upwind for |C|≤1.
Smooth refinement uses N=32,64,128,256, a=1, Courant=0.6, and T=0.37. The
computed value errors approach order three for both gradient initializations;

## CIP: carry the value and the gradient — Reproducible scalar tests# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/cip/#reproducible-scalar-tests
Coverage: reading

the gradient errors are recorded separately. A cubic interpolant alone is
not a fourth-order global-accuracy claim after repeated remapping. Integer
Courant shifts are a special exact-translation case, so they are not used
to infer a generic refinement order. No equal-cost ranking is made between
the N-state linear method and the 2N-state CIP method.

## CIP: carry the value and the gradient — Why a sine wave is not a conservation proof# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/cip/#why-a-sine-wave-is-not-a-conservation-proof
Coverage: reading

The exact integral of the periodic piecewise-Hermite reconstruction is
M=\sum_i\left[\frac h2(f_i+f_{i+1})+
\frac{h^2}{12}(g_i-g_{i+1})\right]=h\sum_i f_i.
For uniform constant-speed remapping with fraction s, its one-step change is
\Delta M=h^2\,[H_{10}(s)+H_{11}(s)]\sum_i g_i.
The initial analytic sine slopes and centered differences sum to zero, so
the displayed scalar runs can conserve this integral to roundoff even though
the method has no universal conservative remapping property.
The separate counterexample uses N=32 and a valid periodic C1 Hermite field
with f_i=1 and g_i=1 at every node. This is not a constant function:
each interval contains a small cubic ripple, and its derivative varies
between the nodes. Its exact integral is 1. Exact translation preserves that
integral, while one CIP remapping step at C=0.35 gives
s=0.65,\qquad \Delta M=h\,s(1-s)(1-2s)=-0.0021328125.
The plot shows the exact shifted original reconstruction and the reconstructed
CIP field over the first four intervals. This is an intentionally constructed
grid-scale test of a claimed property, not a prediction of the mass error for
every smooth flow. Integrals are evaluated analytically, not by coarse
quadrature. Small errors in an easy test cannot establish a stronger guarantee.

## CIP: carry the value and the gradient — Conservative and shape-preserving branches# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/cip/#conservative-and-shape-preserving-branches
Coverage: reading

CIP–CSL (Yabe et al., 2001)
introduces an integral constraint and conservative semi-Lagrangian transport.
Rational CIP / RCIP changes the reconstruction, and variants apply additional
shape constraints. Conservation and boundedness require their own definitions
and tests; neither follows solely from the CIP name.
This edition implements the original 1D cubic only. CIP–CSL2/CSL4, RCIP,
fluid advection/non-advection splitting, multidimensional mixed derivatives,
and complete compressible or multiphase solvers are reading context. The
existing Euler shock-tube solvers retain their documented reconstruction and
flux choices.

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/
Coverage: reading

The formulas below use physical components in the orthonormal basis (e_r,e_phi,e_z), with cylindrical coordinates (r,phi,z), phi in radians, and r > 0. A planar polar field is obtained by setting u_z = 0 and all z derivatives to zero. Coordinate-basis tensor components have different metric factors; mixing the conventions creates incorrect viscous forces.
THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data
For a reference derivation of cylindrical fluid equations, see Richard Fitzpatrick’s lecture notes. This chapter states a general bulk-viscosity convention explicitly and checks it with analytic fields.

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Velocity gradient: differentiate the basis too# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/#velocity-gradient-differentiate-the-basis-too
Coverage: reading

Let L_ij = e_i · ((e_j · grad)u). Its rows are velocity components and columns are differentiation directions:
L=\begin{pmatrix}
\partial_r u_r & (\partial_\phi u_r-u_\phi)/r & \partial_z u_r\\
\partial_r u_\phi & (\partial_\phi u_\phi+u_r)/r & \partial_z u_\phi\\
\partial_r u_z & (\partial_\phi u_z)/r & \partial_z u_z
\end{pmatrix}.
The terms −u_phi/r and +u_r/r arise from rotation of the basis. Define D = (L+L^T)/2 and theta = tr(L):
\theta=\nabla\cdot u=\partial_r u_r+\frac{u_r}{r}
+\frac{\partial_\phi u_\phi}{r}+\partial_z u_z.
The input partials[...,i,j] in numart.coordinates means the plain coordinate derivative of physical velocity component i with respect to coordinate j = (r,phi,z). Supply the phi derivative itself, not a derivative already divided by r.

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Newtonian stress: all six independent components# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/#newtonian-stress-all-six-independent-components
Coverage: reading

With total stress sigma = −p I + tau, dynamic shear viscosity mu, and bulk viscosity zeta, the three-dimensional constitutive law is
\tau=2\mu D+\lambda\theta I,\qquad
\lambda=\zeta-\frac23\mu.
Stokes’ hypothesis sets zeta = 0. It is a material assumption, distinct from imposing incompressibility theta = 0. Positive mu and nonnegative zeta ensure nonnegative viscous dissipation.
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{rr}&=2\mu\,\partial_r u_r+\lambda\theta,\\
\tau_{\phi\phi}&=\frac{2\mu}{r}(u_r+\partial_\phi u_\phi)+\lambda\theta,\\
\tau_{zz}&=2\mu\,\partial_z u_z+\lambda\theta,\\
\tau_{r\phi}&=\mu\left(\partial_r u_\phi-\frac{u_\phi}{r}
+\frac{\partial_\phi u_r}{r}\right),\\
\tau_{rz}&=\mu(\partial_z u_r+\partial_r u_z),\\
\tau_{\phi z}&=\mu\left(\partial_z u_\phi+\frac{\partial_\phi u_z}{r}\right).
\end{aligned}
The lower indices here label physical components, not covariant coordinate-basis components. Off-diagonal engineering shear rates are twice the corresponding D component; applying another factor of two to the formulas above would be an error.

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Stress divergence: the viscous force per volume# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/#stress-divergence-the-viscous-force-per-volume
Coverage: reading

For a symmetric physical stress tensor, f = div(tau) has components
\begin{aligned}
f_r&=\partial_r\tau_{rr}+\frac1r\partial_\phi\tau_{r\phi}
+\partial_z\tau_{rz}+\frac{\tau_{rr}-\tau_{\phi\phi}}r,\\
f_\phi&=\partial_r\tau_{r\phi}+\frac1r\partial_\phi\tau_{\phi\phi}
+\partial_z\tau_{\phi z}+\frac{2\tau_{r\phi}}r,\\
f_z&=\partial_r\tau_{rz}+\frac1r\partial_\phi\tau_{\phi z}
+\partial_z\tau_{zz}+\frac{\tau_{rz}}r.
\end{aligned}
The acceleration contribution is f/rho. Pressure contributes −grad(p) separately. These divergence formulas allow spatially variable mu and zeta when stress derivatives include their variation. In the Python routine, partials[...,i,j,k] is the coordinate derivative k of physical stress component (i,j).

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Constant viscosity and the vector Laplacian# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/#constant-viscosity-and-the-vector-laplacian
Coverage: reading

Only for constant mu and lambda can the force be simplified to
f=\mu\nabla^2 u+(\mu+\lambda)\nabla\theta.
For a scalar g, let
\Delta_s g=\frac1r\partial_r(r\partial_r g)
+\frac1{r^2}\partial_\phi^2g+\partial_z^2g.
The physical components of the vector Laplacian are
\begin{aligned}
(\nabla^2u)_r&=\Delta_su_r-\frac{u_r}{r^2}
-\frac2{r^2}\partial_\phi u_\phi,\\
(\nabla^2u)_\phi&=\Delta_su_\phi-\frac{u_\phi}{r^2}
+\frac2{r^2}\partial_\phi u_r,\\
(\nabla^2u)_z&=\Delta_su_z.
\end{aligned}
For incompressible constant-viscosity flow, theta vanishes, but the radial and azimuthal vector-Laplacian metric terms remain. For variable coefficients, pulling mu outside derivatives omits terms 2D·grad(mu) and theta grad(lambda). Evaluate the full stress divergence instead.

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Axisymmetry, polar slices, and material acceleration# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/#axisymmetry-polar-slices-and-material-acceleration
Coverage: reading

Axisymmetry removes phi derivatives, not the terms u_r/r, −u_phi/r, or the stress-divergence metric terms. Axisymmetric flow may still have swirl. For a planar polar slice of a three-dimensional Newtonian fluid, retain the 2mu/3 bulk correction and tau_zz = lambda theta. A genuinely two-dimensional constitutive model uses a different deviatoric trace subtraction and must be declared separately.
The scalar advective derivative is D_s/Dt = partial_t + u_r partial_r + (u_phi/r) partial_phi + u_z partial_z. Vector material acceleration has extra radial and azimuthal terms:
a_r=\frac{D_su_r}{Dt}-\frac{u_\phi^2}{r},\qquad
a_\phi=\frac{D_su_\phi}{Dt}+\frac{u_ru_\phi}{r},\qquad
a_z=\frac{D_su_z}{Dt}.
These inertial terms are different from viscous metric terms.

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Coordinate-basis tensors and transformations# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/#coordinate-basis-tensors-and-transformations
Coverage: reading

The cylindrical coordinate basis is (partial_r,partial_phi,partial_z) = (e_r,r e_phi,e_z), with metric diag(1,r²,1). Thus physical u_phi = r u^phi, and physical tau_phi,phi = r² tau^{phi,phi} = tau_{phi,phi}^{coordinate}/r². Covariant, contravariant, and physical arrays cannot be substituted for one another without these factors.
Nonzero Christoffel symbols include Gamma^r_phi,phi = −r and Gamma^phi_r,phi = Gamma^phi_phi,r = 1/r. Covariant differentiation accounts for the same basis changes included explicitly above. The Cartesian transformation uses the orthogonal matrix Q with columns e_r, e_phi, e_z: L_cart = Q L_cyl Q^T and tau_cart = Q tau_cyl Q^T.

## Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity — Analytic checks and the axis# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/coordinates-viscosity/#analytic-checks-and-the-axis
Coverage: reading

Rigid rotation: u_phi = Omega r gives antisymmetric L, D = 0, and zero viscous stress. Using partial_r u_phi alone would incorrectly create shear.
Pipe Poiseuille flow: u_z = Umax(1−r²/R²) gives tau_rz = −2 mu Umax r/R² and f_z = −4 mu Umax/R². Steady axial momentum requires dp/dz = f_z.
Circular Couette flow: u_phi = A r+B/r gives tau_rphi = −2 mu B/r² and zero azimuthal viscous-force divergence away from boundaries.
Cartesian affine fields: random constant Cartesian velocity gradients are transformed into cylindrical data and back. Constant Cartesian stresses have zero divergence after angular basis derivatives are included.
The tests also verify the dissipation identity
\tau:D=2\mu D_{\rm dev}:D_{\rm dev}+\zeta\theta^2\ge0.
These routines require r > 0. At the axis, use regularity and analytic limits rather than replacing r by a small arbitrary number. For a smooth axisymmetric field, u_r and u_phi are O(r), and u_z = u_z(0)+O(r²). Then the axial scalar radial Laplacian tends to 2 partial_r² u_z. Nonaxisymmetric regular Cartesian fields have different component limits; even uniform Cartesian translation need not have u_r = O(r).
import numpy as np
from numart.coordinates import cylindrical_velocity_gradient, newtonian_stress
r, omega = 0.7, 2.0
u = np.array([0., omega*r, 0.])
du = np.zeros((3,3)); du[1,0] = omega
L = cylindrical_velocity_gradient(r, u, du)

## Differential-algebraic equations / DAE — Differential-algebraic equations / DAE [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dae/
Coverage: reading

A DAE combines differential evolution with algebraic constraints. An implicit ODE is not necessarily a DAE; singular dependence on derivatives is central to the distinction.

## Differential-algebraic equations / DAE — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dae/#model
Coverage: reading

Use F(t,y,ẏ)=0. A semi-explicit system ẋ=f(x,z,t), 0=g(x,z,t) with invertible g_z is a representative locally eliminable index-1 case. Several index definitions exist; differentiation index concerns differentiating constraints to obtain an explicit ODE.
F(t,y,\dot y)=0,\qquad \dot y_{n+1}\approx\frac{\alpha_0y_{n+1}+\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_jy_{n+1-j}}{\Delta t},\qquad J_N=F_y+\frac{\alpha_0}{\Delta t}F_{\dot y}.

## Differential-algebraic equations / DAE — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dae/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

BDF methods approximate ẏ from the state history and solve F=0 using Newton iterations. The Newton matrix includes F_y+α₀F_ẏ/Δt. Initial values and derivatives must be consistent with both algebraic constraints and F(t₀,y₀,ẏ₀)=0.

## Differential-algebraic equations / DAE — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dae/#conditions
Coverage: reading

Higher-index systems can contain hidden constraints, drift and degraded error control, requiring index reduction or projection formulations. Smaller ODE time steps alone do not fix these issues. Scale tolerances separately for differential and algebraic variables and their units.

## Differential-algebraic equations / DAE — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dae/#verification
Coverage: reading

For an index-1 system with known solution, measure state error, F residual, algebraic-constraint violation and initialization consistency. Vary steps, nonlinear tolerances and initial perturbations; record constraint drift and termination reasons.

## Double Mach Reflection — Equations and initial states# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/double-mach/#equations-and-initial-states
Coverage: reading

Use gamma = 1.4 on [0,4] × [0,1], with conserved state U = (rho, rho u, rho v, E) and E = p/(gamma−1) + rho(u²+v²)/2. The initial shock intersects the bottom wall at x = 1/6 and makes a 60-degree angle with it:
x_s(y,0)=\frac16+\frac{y}{\sqrt3}.
The post-shock state to its left is (rho,u,v,p) = (8, 8.25 sqrt(3)/2, −4.125, 116.5). The ambient state to its right is (1.4,0,0,1). The upstream sound speed is one, so the shock-normal propagation speed of ten corresponds to Mach 10.
Initial cell states are assigned by the cell-center side of the shock; cut-cell averages are not integrated exactly.
The moving incident-shock line is
x_s(y,t)=\frac16+\frac{y+20t}{\sqrt3}.
These states satisfy the moving Rankine–Hugoniot relation in the shock-normal direction; the automated check uses normal (sqrt(3)/2,−1/2) and speed 10.

## Double Mach Reflection — Boundary conditions and discretization# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/double-mach/#boundary-conditions-and-discretization
Coverage: reading

The left boundary supplies the post-shock state. The right boundary uses zero-gradient outflow. At the bottom, x < 1/6 supplies post-shock data; the remaining wall reflects normal momentum. The top boundary assigns the two states using x_s(1,t). SSPRK2 stages evaluate this boundary at their corresponding stage times.
The calculation uses piecewise-constant finite volumes, a two-wave HLL flux with Davis-type minimum/maximum acoustic speeds, and an unsplit flux divergence. The step is bounded by
\Delta t=C\left[\frac{\max(|u|+c)}{\Delta x}
+\frac{\max(|v|+c)}{\Delta y}\right]^{-1}.
The displayed run has Nx = 256, Ny = 64, delta x = delta y = 1/64, C = 0.4, final time 0.2, and 811 steps. Its minimum final density is 1.4 and minimum final pressure is 1.0. These are measured diagnostics for this run, not a general positivity theorem.

## Double Mach Reflection — Reproduce and inspect# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/double-mach/#reproduce-and-inspect
Coverage: reading

python -m numart.cli run double-mach --n 64 --cfl 0.4 --output outputs/double-mach
Here --n sets Ny and Nx = 4 Ny. The command saves solution.npz, run.json, and double-mach.png. The gallery snapshot includes its run manifest and conserved-state arrays. Array q has shape (Nx,Ny,4); x and y are cell-center coordinates. The manifest records source hashes and the working-tree state at generation time.

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/double-mach/#what-the-figure-establishes
Coverage: reading

The image shows a computed incident/reflected shock pattern, with density and thirty density contours. First-order spatial reconstruction is deliberately diffusive. This grid does not resolve the fine wall jet and roll-up of high-resolution PPM or adaptive calculations. There is no exact final-time solution, grid-convergence study, or digitized original-paper comparison in this exhibit.
Tests check equal-state flux consistency, a periodic uniform state, the incident-shock jump relation, moving-top and reflecting-wall data, and admissible states in a small-grid run. They do not establish convergence of the full reflection pattern. Further work should add higher-order reconstruction, refinement, and independent reference-code comparisons.

## DSMC and kinetic transport — DSMC and kinetic transport [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dsmc/
Coverage: reading

DSMC approximates dilute-gas Boltzmann collisions by stochastic collisions between computational particles. It differs from deterministic pair-potential molecular dynamics and from self-consistent plasma PIC fields.

## DSMC and kinetic transport — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dsmc/#model
Coverage: reading

Consider Boltzmann f with molecular velocity v, acceleration a and collision operator Q. A simulator particle represents F_N physical molecules. In a cell of volume V_c, sample pair collisions according to total cross section σ_T and relative speed g. State the phase-space number-density normalization of f.
\partial_t f+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla_x f+\mathbf a\cdot\nabla_v f=Q(f,f),\qquad P_{\rm pair}\sim \frac{F_N\sigma_T g\,\Delta t}{V_c}.

## DSMC and kinetic transport — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dsmc/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Move particles, apply wall/boundary interactions and sample collisions within cells. A representative no-time-counter algorithm uses a bound on gσ_T for candidate selection and acceptance. Specify hard-sphere, VHS or another collision model, distinguishing Bird’s early construction from later algorithms.

## DSMC and kinetic transport — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dsmc/#conditions
Coverage: reading

DSMC uses dilute-gas and molecular-chaos assumptions. Compare cell size with mean free path and step size with mean collision time; adequate resolution is problem dependent. In low-speed flow, the macroscopic signal can be buried in thermal noise, and longer averaging does not remove discretization bias.
The companion consists of homogeneous Maxwell-molecule elastic pair-collision rounds without positions. It is distinct from physical-time no-time-counter transport with cross sections/relative speeds, spatial hard-sphere motion, walls or inflow boundaries.

## DSMC and kinetic transport — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/dsmc/#verification
Coverage: reading

Test homogeneous velocity relaxation, Maxwellian equilibrium, wall-driven Couette flow or a rarefied shock. Check collision-level momentum/energy conservation, cell/step/particle-count sensitivity and uncertainty accounting for correlated samples.
Derive moments on the finite-particle sphere with fixed momentum/energy here, comparing collision samples with independently projected and normalized Gaussian samples. Scalas et al. provide context for finite microcanonical distributions versus thermodynamic limits; this does not reproduce their complete hard-sphere calculation. Separate between-seed uncertainty and particle-count effects from momentum/energy conservation at each collision.
For the finite system with fixed momentum/energy, a suitably normalized squared velocity component has a Beta distribution. Use this finite-particle reference for 16/64/256 particles and 64 seeds, separating finite-N bias relative to the Maxwell limit from sampling error. The distribution comparison follows 24 collision rounds; rounds are not converted into physical time.

## Krylov eigenvalue solvers — Krylov eigenvalue solvers [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/eigensolvers/
Coverage: reading

Krylov eigensolvers approximate a few eigenpairs through a small subspace instead of diagonalizing a large matrix in full. Arnoldi, symmetric Lanczos and shift-invert require different assumptions.

## Krylov eigenvalue solvers — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/eigensolvers/#model
Coverage: reading

Build Kₘ(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Aᵐ⁻¹v}. Arnoldi gives an orthonormal Vₘ and upper-Hessenberg Hₘ. Solve Hₘy=θy and set x=Vₘy. The last Arnoldi vector and hₘ₊₁,ₘ give the Ritz residual.
AV_m=V_mH_m+h_{m+1,m}v_{m+1}e_m^T,\qquad \|Ax-\theta x\|_2=|h_{m+1,m}e_m^Ty|\quad(\|y\|_2=1).

## Krylov eigenvalue solvers — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/eigensolvers/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Expand the basis using matrix-vector products and orthogonalization, solve the projected eigenproblem and restart when needed. Hermitian matrices permit a Lanczos three-term recurrence. Shift-invert targets interior eigenvalues but each inverse action requires a linear solve.

## Krylov eigenvalue solvers — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/eigensolvers/#conditions
Coverage: reading

Finite-precision loss of orthogonality can create ghost duplicates. For nonnormal matrices, a small residual need not imply a comparably small eigenvalue error. State B and the inner product in generalized problems Ax=λBx, and assess inner-solve tolerances for shift-invert.
A small eigen-residual supplies backward-error information about an eigenpair of a nearby matrix; it need not imply small eigenvalue or eigenvector forward error for a nonnormal matrix. Individual-vector matching can be unstable in a close cluster, where principal angles between invariant subspaces can be more appropriate.

## Krylov eigenvalue solvers — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/eigensolvers/#verification
Coverage: reading

Check scaled residuals ∥Ax−θx∥/(∥A∥+|θ|), orthogonality, known eigenpairs and clustered/repeated eigenvalues. For symmetric cases compare Rayleigh quotients, and record restarts and initial-vector sensitivity.
The added release separates eigenvalue spacing from nonnormality on small matrices and compares eigenvalue/subspace errors with independent references as Krylov dimension and residual vary. Passing a residual check alone is not presented as an accurate true eigenvalue. Report conditioning alongside measured errors in clustered and nonnormal controls; no guarantee for arbitrary large nonsymmetric systems is implied. Projected solves and dense references may share LAPACK infrastructure and are not described as fully independent backends. Analytic eigenvalues and constructed pseudoeigenpair controls provide additional checks.

Interior/clustered eigenvalues, very large sparse matrices, strong nonnormality, shift-invert and implicitly restarted Arnoldi are outside scope. A small eigenpair residual alone is not treated as a rigorous eigenvalue-error bound for nonnormal matrices.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Parabolic problems: evolving diffusion# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#parabolic-problems-evolving-diffusion
Coverage: reading

Solve u_t=νu_xx on [0,1] with zero Dirichlet boundaries and initial data
sin(πx). The reference solution is u=exp(-νπ²t)sin(πx).
numart.linear.diffusion_1d returns interior nodes.
Second-order centered differences and the θ method give
(I-\theta\nu\Delta t D_{xx})u^{n+1}
=(I+(1-\theta)\nu\Delta t D_{xx})u^n.
θ=0: FTCS, requiring r=νΔt/h²≤1/2.
θ=1: backward Euler, first order in time and unconditionally stable for linear diffusion.
θ=1/2: Crank–Nicolson, second order in time and A-stable for linear diffusion.
The Fourier amplification factor is
G=[1-4(1-θ)r sin²(ξ/2)]/[1+4θr sin²(ξ/2)].
For large r, Crank–Nicolson can have negative G: high-frequency modes alternate
sign while remaining stable. Stability, positivity, monotonicity, and temporal
resolution need separate checks.
Crank–Nicolson (1947).
spectral_diffusion solves a separate periodic problem by multiplying each
Fourier coefficient by exp(-νk²t). Accuracy comparisons with the Dirichlet
finite-difference problem must account for their different boundaries.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Thomas elimination: from implicit steps to tridiagonal systems# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#thomas-elimination-from-implicit-steps-to-tridiagonal-systems
Coverage: reading

For subdiagonal a, diagonal b, and superdiagonal c, forward elimination uses
m_i=a_i/b'_{i-1}, b'_i=b_i-m_i c_{i-1}, and
d'_i=d_i-m_i d'_{i-1}. Back substitution uses
x_i=(d'_i-c_i x_{i+1})/b'_i. Both work and storage are O(N).
thomas preserves its inputs and raises an error for a small pivot. It uses
elimination without pivoting, so it is not safe for every tridiagonal matrix.
The diffusion matrices used here are strictly diagonally dominant. The original
1949 Thomas report has not been inspected; the historical citation and the
verification of this modern implementation are separate claims.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Elliptic problems: the Poisson equation# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#elliptic-problems-the-poisson-equation
Coverage: reading

The sign convention is -Δu=f. In 1D, use a tridiagonal system and Thomas
elimination; in 2D, use a five-point stencil with matrix-free conjugate gradients
or multigrid. Default manufactured solutions are sin(πx) in 1D and
sin(πx)sin(πy) in 2D. Check the linear-system residual separately from the
discretization error relative to the continuous solution.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundaries# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#dirichlet-neumann-and-robin-boundaries
Coverage: reading

Dirichlet specifies u=g_D; Neumann specifies the outward normal derivative
∂u/∂n=g_N; Robin specifies αu+β∂u/∂n=g. The normal derivative is -u_x at
the left end and +u_x at the right. Outward conductive heat flux is
-k∂u/∂n, so both the specified quantity and its sign matter.
Pass Boundary.dirichlet(value), Boundary.neumann(value), or
Boundary(alpha,beta,value) to poisson_boundary_1d. Robin and Neumann
conditions eliminate ghost points and use half weights at the endpoints.
The time-dependent diffusion_1d currently supports zero Dirichlet boundaries.
A pure-Neumann Poisson solution is determined only up to an additive constant.
The divergence theorem requires
\int_\Omega f\,dV=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g_N\,dS.
The implementation checks the discrete compatibility condition corresponding
to trapezoidal quadrature and fixes the constant with a prescribed mean,
defaulting to zero. Some Robin coefficients also lead to a loss of uniqueness.
Periodic Poisson problems similarly need zero-mode compatibility and a mean
constraint, with the endpoints identified.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Spectral radius of the iteration matrix# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#spectral-radius-of-the-iteration-matrix
Coverage: reading

For a stationary iteration x^{k+1}=T x^k+c solving Ax=b, errors satisfy
e^{k+1}=T e^k. In finite dimensions, convergence for every initial error is
equivalent to ρ(T)<1, where ρ(T)=max |λ_i(T)|.
This differs from the radius of convergence of a power series,
R=1/limsup |a_n|^{1/n}, and from a Newton iteration's basin of convergence.
With A=D+L+U, Jacobi has T=-D^{-1}(L+U), Gauss–Seidel has
T=-(D+L)^{-1}U, and SOR has
T=(D+ωL)^{-1}[(1-ω)D-ωU]. iteration_matrix and spectral_radius support
small-matrix demonstrations. Nonnormal matrices can exhibit transient error
growth even when ρ<1. The system condition number κ(A) and iteration
spectral radius ρ(T) measure different properties.
Netlib Templates.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Red-black Gauss–Seidel and SOR# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#red-black-gaussseidel-and-sor
Coverage: reading

Color the five-point grid with (i+j) mod 2. Updates of one color depend only
on the other color; update red, then black. Set ω=1 for Gauss–Seidel and
use 0<ω<2 for SOR relaxation. This interval alone does not guarantee
convergence for arbitrary nonsymmetric systems. The implementation targets
symmetric positive-definite Dirichlet Poisson problems.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Geometric multigrid V-cycle# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#geometric-multigrid-v-cycle
Coverage: reading

Apply three red-black Gauss–Seidel sweeps on the fine grid.
Compute r_h=f_h-A_h u_h.
Restrict the residual by full weighting.
Solve the coarse-grid error equation recursively.
Prolongate the correction bilinearly.
Apply three more fine-grid sweeps.
Each side has N=2^k-1 interior nodes. Coarse grids use rediscretized five-point
operators, and the one-unknown coarsest problem is solved directly. Tests check
interpolation, restriction, grid spacing, and boundary consistency. Variable
coefficients, anisotropy, curved grids, AMG, and FAS are outside this edition.
Fedorenko (1961),
Brandt (1977).
For a teaching path, start with Briggs–Henson–McCormick, A Multigrid Tutorial, second edition (2000), then use Trottenberg–Oosterlee–Schüller, Multigrid for local Fourier analysis, algorithm design and advanced applications. The textbook guide explains where each book fits. Their broader scope includes methods beyond the geometric V-cycle implemented here.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Particle and disk gravity# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#particle-and-disk-gravity
Coverage: reading

The new particle-gravity chapter connects PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid. Gravity boundary kernels adds Hockney–Eastwood isolated convolution and Koyama–Ostriker slab Fourier kernels. The existing multigrid example retains its 2D zero-Dirichlet operator; it is not a 3D open-boundary gravity solver.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Further routes to diffusion and elliptic problems# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#further-routes-to-diffusion-and-elliptic-problems
Coverage: reading

See continuous P1 FEM for weak-form assembly,
GMRES/ILU and nonlinear solves for nonsymmetric systems,
and Nishikawa hyperbolic diffusion for auxiliary-gradient
pseudo-time iteration. The equation gallery separately
shows physical-time heat diffusion.
For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms,
see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Same-system Poisson comparison# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#same-system-poisson-comparison
Coverage: reading

Open the Poisson solver notebook. All 2D methods solve
one constant-coefficient five-point SPD system on the unit square with zero
Dirichlet boundaries. N=31,63,127 counts interior nodes per side, hence
N² unknowns. Every iterative method starts from zero. The common stopping
criterion uses the explicitly recomputed true residual, including for CG:
 (A_hu)_{ij}=\frac{4u_{ij}-u_{i-1,j}-u_{i+1,j}-u_{i,j-1}-u_{i,j+1}}{h^2},\quad
 h=\frac1{N+1},\qquad
 \frac{\|f-A_hu\|_2}{\|f\|_2}\le 10^{-8}.
Forcing choices are a broad smooth manufactured field and two localized
opposite-sign sources. The manufactured solution is
u=x(1−x)e^(2x)y(1−y)e^(−1.5y), with f=−Δu differentiated analytically.
The localized forcing is
100exp(−[(x−0.28)²+(y−0.35)²]/0.006)
−60exp(−[(x−0.70)²+(y−0.65)²]/0.012), with no continuous exact solution supplied.
Algebraic error is nodal RMS against the FFT/DST discrete solution;
continuous nodal RMS for the manufactured field measures discretization error.
Neither is a continuous integral L2 norm. Tight residuals do not remove
second-order discretization error.
The separate N=31 single-sine diagnostic uses u=sin(πx)sin(πy) and f=2π²u.
It is one eigenvector of this discrete matrix: exact-arithmetic CG requires
one iteration from zero. It is therefore unsuitable as the sole general
solver benchmark. Broad forcing avoids this shortcut.

## Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration — Same-system Poisson comparison# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/elliptic/#same-system-poisson-comparison
Coverage: reading

The compared configurations are Jacobi, weighted Jacobi (ω=2/3), red-black
Gauss–Seidel, red-black SOR, unpreconditioned CG, the existing geometric
multigrid V-cycle, DST+Thomas and FFT/DST direct elimination. SOR uses
ω=2/[1+sin(π/(N+1))] for this model and ordering. This is not a generally
optimal setting for arbitrary meshes/operators. A sweep, CG iteration and
V-cycle are different work units. Multigrid has three pre/post RBGS sweeps
at every level and additional coarse-grid work. Its cycle count is not a
fine-grid sweep count. Netlib's SOR discussion
provides the method context.
The FFT route uses an orthonormal DST-I computed with an odd extension and
NumPy FFT, following the DST-I definition.
The 1D eigenvalues of the difference operator are
λk=4h⁻²sin²[kπ/(2(N+1))]; in 2D divide by λk+λl.
This solves the same discrete operator, rather than substituting continuum
wave numbers k². Zero Dirichlet boundaries are not periodic boundaries.

## Equation gallery: choose the equation before the algorithm — Burgers: shocks and fans# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/equation-gallery/#burgers-shocks-and-fans
Coverage: reading

Burgers (1948) is the classical
model reference; this exhibit uses its inviscid scalar conservation law:
u_t+(u^2/2)_x=0,\qquad f'(u)=u.
A decreasing jump forms a shock traveling at (u_L+u_R)/2. An increasing jump
forms a rarefaction fan, with u=x/t in coordinates centered on the initial
jump. Exact Godunov flux selects the entropy solution, including zero flux
inside a transonic Burgers fan. The plotted exact curves are cell integrals,
so a shock cutting a cell is not treated as a point sample.

## Equation gallery: choose the equation before the algorithm — Traffic: a jam can move against the cars# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/equation-gallery/#traffic-a-jam-can-move-against-the-cars
Coverage: reading

Lighthill–Whitham (1955) and
Richards (1956) are the independent
classical traffic references. This exhibit chooses a normalized quadratic
fundamental diagram, rather than asserting that every traffic model has it:
\rho_t+[\rho(1-\rho)]_x=0,\qquad 0\leq\rho\leq1.
Vehicles move at 1−ρ, while small density disturbances move at 1−2ρ.
A jump from 0.3 to 0.9 shocks at speed −0.2, despite positive vehicle speeds.
The opposite ordering creates a clearing fan because the flux is concave.
Both Burgers and traffic use MUSCL minmod, Godunov flux, SSPRK3 and CFL≤0.4.
Density bounds are checked; the solver does not silently clip them.

## Ewald summation — Ewald summation [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/ewald/
Coverage: reading

Ewald summation evaluates periodic Coulomb interactions through complementary real- and reciprocal-space sums. It defines a different boundary-value problem from simply truncating 1/r at a finite radius.

## Ewald summation — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/ewald/#model
Coverage: reading

Consider point charges qᵢ in a neutral, triply periodic cell. Set rᵢⱼₙ=rᵢ−rⱼ+n, cell volume V, splitting parameter α>0 and reciprocal vector k. S(k) is the charge structure factor. The energy below uses unit Coulomb prefactor, omits k=0 and assumes a conducting macroscopic boundary. The prime excludes only i=j,n=0.
\begin{aligned}S(\mathbf k)&=\sum_jq_j e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r_j},\\E&=\frac12\sum_{i,j,\mathbf n}^{\prime}q_iq_j\frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha r_{ij\mathbf n})}{r_{ij\mathbf n}}+\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{\mathbf k\ne0}\frac{e^{-k^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{k^2}|S(\mathbf k)|^2-\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_iq_i^2.\end{aligned}

## Ewald summation — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/ewald/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Accumulate screened real-space pairs and Gaussian-damped reciprocal modes, then subtract the self energy. Restore the same Coulomb prefactor to every term in dimensional units. Changing α redistributes work between sums but cannot change their converged total. Derive forces from the same energy convention.

## Ewald summation — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/ewald/#conditions
Coverage: reading

A net-charged cell requires an additional convention such as a compensating background. Specify potential gauge, surface term, periodic self images and molecular exclusions separately. A periodic gravitational Poisson solve changes the kernel/sign and mean-density treatment; it is not the same calculation.
The companion release keeps an asymmetric neutral eight-charge cubic cell, triply periodic with tin-foil boundaries. It separates the direct-Ewald splitting parameter, real-image and reciprocal-cube cutoffs, using a separately implemented heat-kernel theta integral as a reference. It does not extend to charged backgrounds or slabs.

## Ewald summation — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/ewald/#verification
Coverage: reading

For a small neutral configuration, increase both cutoffs independently and test α independence. Compare forces with finite differences of energy, and check translation invariance and net force. Agreement between two unconverged sums is not independent validation.
Historical and companion inputs, criteria and results are retained separately. The companion checks energy and every particle force, refinement of the reference integral itself, translations, particle ordering, net force and energy differences individually; a deliberately truncated control is distinct from a converged reference.

## Interactive experiment guide — Periodic advection in the browser# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/experiments/#periodic-advection-in-the-browser
Coverage: reading

The model is
u_t+a u_x=0,\qquad x\in[0,1],\qquad u(x+1,t)=u(x,t).
Use 64 cell-centered sample points, h=1/64, velocity a=+1 or a=-1,
and Δt=|C|h. The signed Courant number is C=aΔt/h. The controls expose
0.05≤|C|≤1.5 and 0–100 time steps. The exact comparison samples the
continuous translated profile u(x-at,0) at the same grid points.
Initial data can be a sine wave, a square pulse equal to one on [0.25,0.65)
and zero elsewhere, or a sine wave with small high-frequency perturbations:
u(x,0)=\sin(2\pi x)+10^{-3}
\left[\sin(2\pi(N/2)x)+\cos(2\pi(N/4)x)\right].
The ripple seeds both Nyquist and shorter resolved grid-scale modes. It makes
unstable growth visible without relying on machine roundoff. The square
pulse illustrates smearing and dispersive oscillations; it is not a smooth
convergence test.

## Interactive experiment guide — Four discrete updates# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/experiments/#four-discrete-updates
Coverage: reading

numart.advection.difference_step and the browser implement FTCS, upwind,
classical Lax–Friedrichs, and Lax–Wendroff. Upwind switches stencil with the
velocity sign. The stability chapter develops their context.
For FTCS,
u_j^{n+1}=u_j^n-\frac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n),\qquad
G(\theta)=1-iC\sin\theta.
Its squared amplification is 1+C²sin²θ. Consequently, nonzero C produces
growing modes even when the necessary domain-of-dependence bound |C|≤1
is met. Upwind, LF, and LW satisfy the Fourier stability criterion for this
periodic constant-coefficient problem when |C|≤1.
The solution plot updates alongside |G(θ)|. The reported maximum samples
all distinct real-data Fourier wavenumbers of the 64-point grid. The dashed
threshold marks |G|=1. When the solution grows, its vertical scale expands
rather than clipping the computed values. Pointwise L1 error, maximum
amplitude, and arithmetic mean drift are reported separately.
These properties concern this linear periodic model. They do not transfer
automatically to nonlinear systems, other boundaries, or a different time
integrator. With unstable growth, cancellation and floating-point rounding
can also corrupt the measured mean.

## Interactive experiment guide — Reproducibility and export# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/experiments/#reproducibility-and-export
Coverage: reading

The browser kernels are compared with 24 reference cases generated from the
Python implementation: four methods, six signed Courant numbers, and twelve
updates per case. Tests compare complete sample arrays and complex Fourier
amplification factors. Separate tests check exact one-cell translation at
unit CFL, direction reversal, periodic wrapping, and observed-order arithmetic.
The fixture records the SHA-256 of numart/advection.py; a source mismatch
fails the browser numerical tests until the reference export is refreshed.
The experiment download contains settings, grid coordinates, initial,
computed, and exact samples, diagnostics, and the Python reference hash.
It records a calculation performed in JavaScript, rather than claiming that
Python runs in the browser.
To apply the same stencil from Python:
import numpy as np
from numart.advection import difference_step
n, courant, steps = 64, 0.8, 40
x = (np.arange(n) + 0.5) / n
q = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
for _ in range(steps):
 q = difference_step(q, courant, "lax-wendroff")
exact = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (x - courant * steps / n))
print("pointwise L1 error:", np.mean(abs(q - exact)))

For successive meshes, the displayed observed order is
p_{\mathrm{obs}}=
\frac{\log(E_{\mathrm{coarse}}/E_{\mathrm{fine}})}
{\log(N_{\mathrm{fine}}/N_{\mathrm{coarse}})}.
DG advection: periodic scalar transport, final time 0.2, CFL 0.2,
N=8,16,32,64, modal Legendre P0/P1/P2, and SSPRK3. The error is RMS sampled
at the implementation's quadrature points. It is not a separately integrated
L2 norm. Pp stores N(p+1) scalar unknowns. Toggle the horizontal axis between
elements and unknowns; the data remain unchanged. Spatial orders 1, 2, and 3
and SSPRK3's time order three explain the expected smooth behavior.
Euler entropy wave: final time 1, CFL 0.3, N=40,80,160, primitive minmod
MUSCL or componentwise FD WENO5-JS with SSPRK3. The error is pointwise density
L1. WENO's fifth-order spatial reconstruction does not remove the third-order
time error, so slopes from this finite sequence do not guarantee asymptotic
fifth-order fully discrete convergence. Euler stores three scalar state
components per point or cell; equal counts do not imply equal computational
cost or identical approximation spaces.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Model, units and scope [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#model
Coverage: reading

\partial_t E_z=\partial_xH_y-\partial_yH_x,\qquad \partial_tH_x=-\partial_yE_z,\qquad \partial_tH_y=\partial_xE_z,\quad \epsilon=\mu=c=1.
Length, time and fields are normalized so ε=μ=c=1. The rectangle has Lx=1 and Ly=1.5, with mode indices (m,l)=(1,1). An oblique periodic mode on a rectangular domain exercises both spatial derivatives and magnetic-field signs. These initial vacuum examples exclude dispersion, loss, interfaces and external excitation; later examples cover their stated additional scopes.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Yee placement and staggered time update [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

\begin{aligned}H_{x,i,j+1/2}^{n+1/2}&=H_{x,i,j+1/2}^{n-1/2}-\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta y}(E_{i,j+1}^{n}-E_{i,j}^{n}),\\H_{y,i+1/2,j}^{n+1/2}&=H_{y,i+1/2,j}^{n-1/2}+\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x}(E_{i+1,j}^{n}-E_{i,j}^{n}),\\E_{i,j}^{n+1}&=E_{i,j}^{n}+\Delta t\left(\frac{H_{y,i+1/2,j}^{n+1/2}-H_{y,i-1/2,j}^{n+1/2}}{\Delta x}-\frac{H_{x,i,j+1/2}^{n+1/2}-H_{x,i,j-1/2}^{n+1/2}}{\Delta y}\right).\end{aligned}
Ez lives at nodes and integer times; Hx is displaced by half a y cell and Hy by half an x cell, both at half-integer times. Each step advances H first and then E. Initial E at time zero and H at −Δt/2 are sampled from analytic fields; assigning both fields time zero would introduce a first-order initialization error.
Periodic arrays omit duplicate endpoints and wrap differences. PEC walls fix tangential Ez=0 and update only interior electric nodes. Half weights for boundary magnetic samples make the weighted inner products compatible with discrete summation by parts and the energy identity.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Continuum periodic plane wave [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#periodic-mode
Coverage: reading

\begin{gathered}k_x=2\pi m/L_x,\quad k_y=2\pi l/L_y,\quad\omega=\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2},\quad\phi=k_xx+k_yy-\omega t,\\ E_z=\cos\phi,\quad H_x=(k_y/\omega)\cos\phi,\quad H_y=-(k_x/\omega)\cos\phi.\end{gathered}
Evaluate the electric and both magnetic fields at their own spatial locations and times. Frequency supplies a phase-speed error separate from field error. A sampled continuum magnetic field need not have exactly zero discrete divergence, so the continuum-initialized run checks preservation of its initial divergence.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Continuum PEC cavity eigenmode [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#cavity-mode
Coverage: reading

\begin{gathered}k_x=m\pi/L_x,\quad k_y=l\pi/L_y,\quad\omega=\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2},\\E_z=\sin(k_xx)\sin(k_yy)\cos(\omega t),\\H_x=-\frac{k_y}{\omega}\sin(k_xx)\cos(k_yy)\sin(\omega t),\quad H_y=\frac{k_x}{\omega}\cos(k_xx)\sin(k_yy)\sin(\omega t).\end{gathered}
This standing wave has Ez=0 on all four walls. It uses a different boundary implementation from the periodic wave, with checks of maximum wall electric field, eigenfrequency and field error. The cavity here is a z-invariant two-dimensional section; it does not cover the full three-dimensional cavity spectrum.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — CFL condition and discrete dispersion [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#conditions
Coverage: reading

\frac{\sin^2(\omega_h\Delta t/2)}{\Delta t^2}=\frac{\sin^2(k_x\Delta x/2)}{\Delta x^2}+\frac{\sin^2(k_y\Delta y/2)}{\Delta y^2},\qquad S=\Delta t\sqrt{\Delta x^{-2}+\Delta y^{-2}}<1.
The fixed input sets a Courant-number ceiling of 0.7; S≥1 is rejected. Rounding the required step count upward and choosing Δt from that count reaches the prescribed 1.1-period comparison time exactly, with actual S at or slightly below 0.7. Refining the grid also refines the time step, so measured orders describe coupled spatial and temporal refinement. They are not separate experimental estimates of spatial order and temporal order.
A three-time-level recurrence for evolved modal projection coefficients measures frequency. Its convergence toward continuum ω is separate from agreement with discrete ωh. Additional tests initialize magnetic amplitudes with the discrete wave numbers and check the exact discrete eigenmode to roundoff accuracy.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Discrete invariant versus physical energy [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#energy
Coverage: reading

\begin{aligned}U_*^n&=\frac12\lVert E^n\rVert_h^2+\frac12\langle H^{n-1/2},H^{n+1/2}\rangle_h=\mathrm{constant},\\\bar H^n&=(H^{n-1/2}+H^{n+1/2})/2,\\ U_{\rm sync}^n&=\tfrac12(\lVert E^n\rVert_h^2+\lVert\bar H^n\rVert_h^2),\\ U_*^n&=U_{\rm sync}^n-\frac{\Delta t^2}{8}\lVert\operatorname{curl}_h E^n\rVert_h^2.\end{aligned}
Inner products include cell area and the appropriate PEC boundary weights. U*, containing magnetic fields from two different half times, is conserved up to roundoff in the closed periodic/PEC systems. The strict CFL inequality also ensures positivity of this modified energy. Usync, using magnetic fields averaged to an integer time, is a second-order approximation to physical energy but is not exactly invariant.
For unit-amplitude continuum fields the total energies are LxLy/2 for the traveling periodic wave and LxLy/8 for the cavity standing wave. Twelve periods are used to track relative U* drift and the variation of Usync; the error against the analytic physical energy must decrease at approximately second order under grid/time refinement. Tests also check U* conservation with compatible random fields, beyond single eigenmodes.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Revision r6: lossy and dispersive media [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#interface-loss-dispersion
Coverage: reading

A one-dimensional packet is normally incident on a finite slab surrounded by vacuum. Two examples use Ohmic conductivity and one damped Lorentz resonance. Ez, polarization P and polarization current J occupy integer times; Hy occupies half times. A Yee magnetic step is followed by a local implicit-midpoint E/P/J solve.
\begin{gathered}\epsilon_\infty\partial_t E=\partial_xH-\sigma E-J,\quad\partial_tH=\partial_xE,\\\partial_tP=J,\quad\partial_tJ=fE-\omega_0^2P-\gamma J,\quad f=\Delta\epsilon\,\omega_0^2,\\\epsilon(\omega)=\epsilon_\infty+\frac{f}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2-i\gamma\omega}+\frac{i\sigma}{\omega},\quad e^{-i\omega t}.\end{gathered}
σ multiplies the conventional current σE. When f=0, P=J=0 and oscillator terms are omitted. Distant PEC caps close the domain, with no PML in this example. Interface electric control volumes use half-volume averages of ε∞, σ and f.
The analytic solution includes internal multiple reflections and a complex wavenumber, weighted by the actual incident spectrum. Numerical R/T come from exterior Poynting fluences; A comes from directly accumulated conductive and polarization damping work. Absorption and transient material storage are separated, with energy budgets and spatial/temporal refinement checked.
Finest-grid finite-window measurements and spectrum-weighted analytic values.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Revision r6: lossy and dispersive media [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#interface-loss-dispersion
Coverage: reading

\begin{gathered}U_*^n=\tfrac12\|E^n\|_{\epsilon_\infty,h}^2+\tfrac12\Re\langle H^{n-1/2},H^{n+1/2}\rangle_h+U_{\rm mat}^n,\\U_{\rm mat}=\sum_{f_j>0}\frac{|J_j|^2+\omega_0^2|P_j|^2}{2f_j}\Delta x,\\\Delta W_\sigma=\Delta t\sum_j\sigma_j|\bar E_j|^2\Delta x,\quad\Delta W_\gamma=\Delta t\sum_{f_j>0}\frac{\gamma|\bar J_j|^2}{f_j}\Delta x,\\U_*^n+W_\sigma^n+W_\gamma^n=U_*^0.\end{gathered}
Complex fields represent two real quadratures, consistently across energies and fluxes. Wσ/Wγ are computed from midpoint fields, independently of energy deficits and 1−R−T. The modified discrete energy identity and physical local Poynting budget with centered H have separate criteria. Midpoint inner products cancel E–J exchange, and paired discrete curls cancel at PEC caps, giving the identity. The strict CFL uses ε∞, rather than static permittivity: Δt/Δx<min(1,√ε∞). Oscillator storage is not added to absorption.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Fixed inputs and measured results [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#verification
Coverage: reading

Acceptance tolerances are saved in each fixed input. Separate checks require field error ≤0.01, observed orders ≥1.8, relative frequency error ≤0.002, discrete-dispersion identity error ≤10⁻⁹ and relative U* drift ≤2×10⁻¹¹. Separate checks require zero wall electric field, preservation of initial magnetic divergence, maximum Usync error against the analytic total energy ≤0.003, and approximately second-order refinement of that error. The Usync variation span is retained as a diagnostic.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Dielectric interface: Fresnel amplitudes and energy [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#interface
Coverage: reading

\eta_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\epsilon_j},\quad r=\frac{\eta_2-\eta_1}{\eta_2+\eta_1},\quad t=\frac{2\eta_2}{\eta_1+\eta_2},\qquad R=|r|^2,\quad T=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}|t|^2,\quad R+T=1.
A Gaussian packet is normally incident on a flat interface between nonmagnetic, lossless, nondispersive media ε₁=1 and ε₂=4, μ=1. The interface x=8 coincides with an electric node, assigned the arithmetic mean permittivity. This is a y-invariant reduction of 2D TMz. Analytic values are r=−1/3, t=2/3, R=1/9 and T=8/9.
The domain is 16×1, initial center x=4, width 0.5, comparison time t=8, with 160/320/640 x cells and 4 y cells. Incident, reflected and transmitted packets have separate continuum formulas; electric amplitudes are measured by projection. Packet-energy R,T are integrated using ε|E|² and magnetic fields, separately from simply squaring amplitudes. The shared interface-node quadrature weight is split between left and right regions.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Left/right x-PML: normal and oblique packets [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#pml
Coverage: reading

\begin{aligned}E_z&=E_x+E_y,\\\partial_t E_x+\gamma_E E_x&=\epsilon^{-1}\partial_xH_y,& \partial_t E_y&=-\epsilon^{-1}\partial_yH_x,\\\partial_t H_y+\gamma_H H_y&=\partial_xE_z,& \partial_t H_x&=-\partial_yE_z,\\\gamma_E&=\sigma_e/\epsilon,\quad\gamma_H=\sigma_m/\mu,\qquad\gamma_E(x)=\gamma_H(x),\quad\mu=1.\end{aligned}\frac{u^{n+1}-u^n}{\Delta t}+\gamma\frac{u^{n+1}+u^n}{2}=D_hv,\qquad u^{n+1}=\frac{1-\gamma\Delta t/2}{1+\gamma\Delta t/2}u^n+\frac{\Delta t}{1+\gamma\Delta t/2}D_hv.
Eₓ and Eᵧ are auxiliary splits of Ez, not physical x/y electric components. A Bérenger-type split-field PML on only the left/right x sides of a y-periodic TMz strip matches damping of the electric split Eₓ and magnetic Hy. Outer caps are PEC. This differs from an isotropic sponge that damps every field component equally.
Physical PML thickness 2, cubic damping profile and maximum rate 10 remain fixed across 384×16,768×32 and 1536×64 grids in a 12×π/4 domain. A Gaussian-weighted sum of 511 positive-kx continuum Fourier modes uses carrier kx=12 and ky=0 or 8. Carrier angles are 0° and about 33.690°, while finite bandwidth gives an angular spectrum. Every mode solves the continuum Maxwell equations exactly; the same finite superposition is the analytic reference.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Left/right x-PML: normal and oblique packets [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#pml
Coverage: reading

Early fields are compared with the continuum mode sum to measure propagation-error refinement. Boundary reflection is isolated by subtracting a PML-free reference on a domain five times as long with identical grid spacing, time step and Yee update at the x=6 monitor. The wide-domain reference isolates boundary effects; it is not an independent external library solver.
\rho_h=\frac{\max_{t\in\mathcal W}\|E_{\rm PML}(x_m,\cdot,t)-E_{\rm wide}(x_m,\cdot,t)\|_{\rm RMS,y}}{\max_t\|E_{\rm wide}(x_m,\cdot,t)\|_{\rm RMS,y}}.
Reflection ρ is the peak returned electric-field RMS over y divided by the peak incident RMS. The fixed measurement window is t=8 through 18. Its square is a squared-amplitude diagnostic, not an upper bound on broadband integrated reflected energy. Refinement holds layer thickness, incident spectrum and the time window fixed.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Energy budgets and revision-r2 reproduction [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/#scattering-verification
Coverage: reading

U_*^n=\tfrac12\lVert E_n\rVert_{\epsilon,h}^2+\tfrac12\langle H^{n-1/2},H^{n+1/2}\rangle_{\mu,h},\quad\mu=1.\begin{aligned}\bar E_n&=(E_{n+1}+E_n)/2,\quad\bar E_{x,n}=(E_{x,n+1}+E_{x,n})/2,\\\bar H_{y,n}&=(H_y^{n-1/2}+H_y^{n+1/2})/2,\\W_n&=\Delta t\langle\bar E_n,\epsilon\gamma_E\bar E_{x,n}\rangle_h+\frac{\Delta t}{2}\langle H_y^{n+1/2},\gamma_H(\bar H_{y,n}+\bar H_{y,n+1})\rangle_h,\\U_*^{n+1}-U_*^n+W_n&=0.\end{aligned}
Here U* is the modified discrete energy weighted by permittivity. Magnetic work uses three consecutive half times, while electric work uses averaged total and split electric fields. Both are tallied directly from fields and damping coefficients, not defined as minus an energy change, allowing an independent balance comparison. Electric split work can be locally signed and is not pointwise positive physical Ohmic heating. Vacuum CFL alone is not claimed to prove positivity for arbitrary strongly damped auxiliary fields.
S_x=-E_zH_y,\qquad U_{\rm physical}(t)-U_{\rm physical}(0)+\int_0^t\!\int_0^{L_y}[S_x(x_R,y,\tau)-S_x(x_L,y,\tau)]\,dy\,d\tau=0.
Coarse meshes did not enter the asymptotic regime for the long round-trip phase error. The final input therefore uses 384×16,768×32 and 1536×64 with unchanged physical layer and acceptance tolerances; earlier trial outcomes were not relabeled as successful.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Directional damping and corner overlap [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/
Coverage: reading

\begin{aligned}E_z&=E_x+E_y,\\\partial_t E_x+\gamma_{x,E}E_x&=\partial_xH_y,&\partial_t E_y+\gamma_{y,E}E_y&=-\partial_yH_x,\\\partial_t H_x+\gamma_{y,H}H_x&=-\partial_yE_z,&\partial_t H_y+\gamma_{x,H}H_y&=\partial_xE_z,\quad\epsilon=\mu=1.\end{aligned}
In the implemented vacuum 2D TMz square, γx layers occupy the left/right sides and γy layers the bottom/top sides. All outer caps are PEC. Both directional rates are nonzero in the four overlap corners. Eₓ and Eᵧ are auxiliary splits of Ez, not physical x/y electric components. Each rate is sampled at its own electric or staggered magnetic location; damping uses the trapezoidal time update.
One packet family targets ordinary sides; another targets corners obliquely. Checks establish more than a decrease in global energy: all four outgoing fluxes and contributions in all four corners are recorded. Physical layer thickness, strength and shape stay fixed during refinement, so changing resolution does not change the physical layer.

## Yee FDTD: foundations and verified examples — Reference waveform and interpretation of reflection [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fdtd/
Coverage: reading

A boundary-free Fourier-mode evolution of the same discrete Maxwell equations separates ordinary propagation dispersion from boundary effects. Its update and time staggering are checked against explicit Yee updates on a separate small periodic grid. Reference period and initial physical/auxiliary split-field tails inside the layers are separately audited to distinguish periodic images from reflected waves. This is not a comparison against an independent external solver library.
The reported boundary-induced probe error normalizes the difference between PML and boundary-free monitor fields by incident amplitude. It includes finite-layer and initial PML/auxiliary-tail effects and is not called a pure ideal-PML reflection coefficient. A finite PEC-backed layer can retain nonzero returns even at very fine resolution. Absolute return amplitude is distinguished from changes of the return waveform under refinement. No zero-reflection guarantee is made outside the observation window or for arbitrary incidence.
Initial fields are standing finite-Fourier packets. Axis carriers center on (±6, 0), (0, ±6); diagonal carriers center on (±4, ±4), producing four outgoing groups. Diagonal carrier directions are 45 degrees; the finite bandwidth is distinct from a single-angle monochromatic plane wave.

The averaged fields and modified energy U* retain their definitions above, but work now includes all four electric-x/y and magnetic-x/y terms. Magnetic work uses three consecutive half times. ## Continuous finite elements: from weak form to sparse assembly — 1943: a variational route# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/fem/#1943-a-variational-route
Coverage: reading

Courant (1943)
is a foundational variational reference. This chapter's small implementation
is an independent modern P1 demonstration, rather than a reproduction of his examples.
For −Δu=f, prescribe u=g on the boundary. Multiplication by a test function
that vanishes there and integration by parts give
\int_\Omega \nabla u_h\cdot\nabla v_h\,d\Omega
=\int_\Omega f v_h\,d\Omega.
Write u_h as nodal coefficients times continuous piecewise linear basis
functions. On a triangle K, the shape gradients are constant:
K^K_{ij}=|K|\nabla\phi_i\cdot\nabla\phi_j,
\qquad M^K_{ij}=\frac{|K|}{12}(1+\delta_{ij}).
Shared nodes accumulate element contributions into CSR storage. Nonzero
Dirichlet values move to the right-hand side before symmetric row/column
elimination. Treating only rows would destroy the symmetry relevant to CG.
The example uses ILU-preconditioned GMRES.

## Flux reconstruction: flux correction, DG and 1D periodic advection — Flux reconstruction: flux correction, DG and 1D periodic advection [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/flux-reconstruction/
Coverage: reading

Flux reconstruction (FR) builds high-order conservation-law discretizations by correcting a polynomial flux inside each element with shared interface fluxes. Elements exchange information through numerical fluxes rather than enforcing a continuous solution. The correction function is part of the method definition; the name FR alone specifies neither accuracy nor stability.

## Flux reconstruction: flux correction, DG and 1D periodic advection — Separate solution points from numerical interface fluxes [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/flux-reconstruction/#local-flux
Coverage: reading

u_t+a u_x=0,\quad x\in[0,1),\quad u(x+1,t)=u(x,t),\quad u_*(x,t)=0.4+\sin(2\pi(x-at))u_h(\xi)=\sum_{j=0}^{p}u_j\ell_j(\xi),\qquad f^D(\xi)=\sum_{j=0}^{p}f(u_j)\ell_j(\xi)
Map each interval to ξ in [−1,1] and store values at p+1 solution points. Extrapolation to a face gives two traces from neighboring elements. For this constant-speed problem choose the left state when a>0 and the right state when a<0, giving one shared upwind flux per face.

## Flux reconstruction: flux correction, DG and 1D periodic advection — Connect face fluxes with correction functions [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/flux-reconstruction/#corrected-flux
Coverage: reading

f^C(\xi)=f^D(\xi)+(f_L^*-f_L^D)g_L(\xi)+(f_R^*-f_R^D)g_R(\xi)g_L(-1)=1,\ g_L(1)=0,\qquad g_R(-1)=0,\ g_R(1)=1,\qquad\dot u_i=-\frac{2}{h}\partial_\xi f^C(\xi_i)
Here fD is the element-local flux polynomial and f* is the shared numerical flux. Distribute their face differences using gL/gR so that the corrected flux matches f* at the endpoints. Differentiate it at the solution points to evolve the state. Distinguish these unknowns and flux corrections from the different reconstruction procedures in MUSCL/WENO.

## Flux reconstruction: flux correction, DG and 1D periodic advection — A Radau choice that recovers DG [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/flux-reconstruction/#dg-connection
Coverage: reading

g_L=\frac{(-1)^p}{2}(P_p-P_{p+1}),\qquad g_R=\frac12(P_p+P_{p+1})M\dot{\mathbf u}=\frac{2}{h}\left[aD^TM\mathbf u-\mathbf t_R f_R^*+\mathbf t_L f_L^*\right],\qquad M=\operatorname{diag}(w_i)
Use Gauss solution points and the displayed Radau corrections. M is the diagonal Gauss-weight matrix, tL/tR extrapolate to faces and D differentiates on the reference interval. For a constant linear flux on affine intervals, this FR formulation corresponds to nodal DG. Modal Legendre coefficients represent the same polynomial when initial projection, flux and time stepping match. Nonlinear flux aliasing, other quadratures and other corrections require separate conditions.

## Flux reconstruction: flux correction, DG and 1D periodic advection — Small example: translate a sine by a quarter period [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/flux-reconstruction/#example
Coverage: reading

Initial 0.4+sin(2pi x), speed 1, T=.25; execute p=1/2 on 8/16/32 cells. Bundle byte-identical published DG modules and run each configuration. During h refinement enforce scaled Courant(2p+1)|a|dt/h<=.15. The final wave has actually moved; the calculation does not use a stationary initial picture as evidence of transport.
Saved initial/final fields and checks. DG differences and mass changes are displayed on axes at the scale of 10⁻¹⁵ roundoff.

## Flux reconstruction: flux correction, DG and 1D periodic advection — Separate conservation, dissipation and time error [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/flux-reconstruction/#conservation
Coverage: reading

I_h=\sum_e\frac{h}{2}\sum_iw_iu_{e,i},\quad \frac{dI_h}{dt}=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\frac12\|u_h\|_{L^2}^2=-\frac{|a|}{2}\sum_{\rm faces}[u_h]^2
Shared face fluxes cancel in the periodic mass balance. The semidiscrete quadratic energy dissipates with interface jumps under upwinding. This does not guarantee stability at arbitrary timesteps or nonlinear entropy stability. Also measure every RK stage’s mass and each completed step’s energy.
\dot U=A_hU,\quad U_{\exp}(T)=\exp(TA_h)U(0),\quad E_t=\|U_{\rm RK3}(T)-U_{\exp}(T)\|_M
Continuous L2 errors use additional Gauss points. Coupled h/dt observed orders are about 1.99 at p1 and 3.00 at p2. The maximum FR/published-DG difference is about 4.0e−15; maximum stage mass change is about 3.6e−15.
Compute an exponential action of the same spatial matrix as a separate time propagator. At p2/N32, RK3 time error is about 9.44e−9 and halves in timestep to 1.18e−9, a ratio about.125. This is not an independent spatial PDE solver. Preserve the initial dense-exponential warning and subsequent JSON scalar-type failure with their original source/input/results; fixes retain every numerical acceptance threshold.

## Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids — Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/geophysical-grids/
Coverage: reading

A/B/C names specify where different variables live on a mesh. They are
not an accuracy order, a mesh shape, or a time-stepping family. A structured
rectangular mesh may use any of these staggerings. The conventional comparison
is described by Arakawa–Lamb (1977),
with a useful agency exposition in the
ECMWF numerical-methods notes.
THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data
Implemented here: spherical mesh geometry diagrams, plus placement diagrams
and tested Fourier symbols for a linear periodic f-plane shallow-water system. This is not an A/B/C nonlinear
weather or ocean model, and it introduces no new full flow simulation.

## Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids — A sphere needs several charts# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/geophysical-grids/#spherical-meshes
Coverage: reading

Mesh geometry and variable staggering are separate choices. A cubed sphere
can carry a C-grid arrangement; a triangular mesh can also store edge-normal
velocities. A/B/C labels alone do not specify spherical connectivity or metrics.
On a sphere of radius R, with latitude φ and longitude λ,
 ds^2=R^2\left(d\varphi^2+\cos^2\varphi\,d\lambda^2\right),
 \qquad \Delta s_\lambda\simeq R\cos\varphi\,\Delta\lambda.
Geographic poles are regular physical locations. Longitude becomes undefined
there, while equal longitude increments become very short near them. An
explicit wave/advection CFL bound can therefore become restrictive. Pole
filters, reduced grids and spectral methods are other responses; replacing
the mesh is not the only option. The three constructions below avoid the
single latitude–longitude chart's polar convergence, while introducing other
coupling and metric questions. None is automatically equal-area.

## Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids — Yin–Yang: two overlapping low-latitude patches# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/geophysical-grids/#yin-yang
Coverage: reading

Kageyama–Sato (2004) combine two
identical latitude–longitude patches. In each patch's own coordinates,
 |\varphi|\leq\pi/4+\delta,\qquad |\lambda|\leq3\pi/4+\delta,
 \qquad
 \boldsymbol{x}^{\mathrm{Yang}}=
 \begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}
 \boldsymbol{x}^{\mathrm{Yin}}.
The rotation puts each chart's poles inside the other chart's low-latitude
region. The figure uses δ=3°; purple marks overlap, not a third patch.
Each component retains orthogonal latitude–longitude coordinates and familiar
metrics. Boundary data must be transferred through the overlap. Interpolating
scalar values alone does not guarantee a globally conservative mass budget;
overlap ownership/weights and conservative coupling need explicit design.
Velocity components must also rotate between local tangent bases. These
transfers are explained here, but no overset transport solver is implemented.

## Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids — Cubed sphere: six connected panels# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/geophysical-grids/#cubed-sphere
Coverage: reading

The six-face construction is associated with
Ronchi–Iacono–Paolucci (1996).
Our diagram chooses equiangular gnomonic coordinates. For an orthonormal
face frame with outward normal n and tangent directions e₁,e₂,
 \boldsymbol{x}(\xi,\eta)=R\,
 \frac{\boldsymbol{n}+\tan\xi\,\boldsymbol{e}_1+\tan\eta\,\boldsymbol{e}_2}
 {\left\lVert\boldsymbol{n}+\tan\xi\,\boldsymbol{e}_1+\tan\eta\,\boldsymbol{e}_2\right\rVert},
 \qquad -\pi/4\leq\xi,\eta\leq\pi/4.
The picture has 8×8 cells per panel. Adjacent panel boundaries match; three
panels meet at each cube corner. This mapping avoids a latitude–longitude
pole but is generally nonorthogonal inside a face, and cell areas and metric
factors vary. Other cubed-sphere projections have different properties.
Neighbor indices, vector components and numerical fluxes must agree across
seams. A continuous-looking diagram is not a test of those operators.

## Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids — Icosahedral triangles and their dual# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/geophysical-grids/#icosahedral
Coverage: reading

Start with 20 triangular faces, split each triangle into four using edge
midpoints, and project new vertices radially onto the sphere. At level L,
 F=20\,4^L,\qquad E=30\,4^L,\qquad V=10\,4^L+2,
 \qquad V-E+F=2.
Level 2 has 320 triangles, 480 edges and 162 vertices. Twelve vertices have
five neighbors; the others have six. Connecting neighboring face centers through shared edge midpoints
produces a dual with twelve pentagons and otherwise hexagons. Here the centers
are normalized triangle centroids: this is a barycentric dual, not a claim
of a Voronoi/Delaunay orthogonal pair. For this unoptimized sample, the largest
triangle area is about 1.275 times the smallest, so quasi-uniform does not mean
equal-area. The connectivity formulas apply to this regular refinement, not
every possible spherical unstructured mesh.
The ICON model description
is a useful example of triangular mesh geometry combined with C-type
staggering. Our illustration is not the optimized ICON mesh or its dynamical
core. Accurate divergence, gradient, vorticity and wave dispersion still
depend on compatible discrete operators.

## Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids — Interfaces, vectors and what the figures verify# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/geophysical-grids/#spherical-interface-checks
Coverage: reading

A physical tangent velocity is one vector, even when its components differ
between charts. If E_A and E_B have orthonormal tangent basis vectors as
columns in one common Cartesian frame, then
 \boldsymbol{v}=E_A\boldsymbol{u}_A=E_B\boldsymbol{u}_B,
 \qquad \boldsymbol{u}_B=E_B^{\mathsf T}E_A\boldsymbol{u}_A.
This formula uses orthonormal physical components. Covariant or contravariant
components in nonorthogonal coordinates require the corresponding metric and
dual basis. Copying two component arrays across a seam is insufficient.
For finite volumes, a shared interface needs the same integrated flux with
opposite signs in neighboring cell budgets. Overset grids additionally need
a well-defined accounting of overlap; summing both full patches counts some
area twice.
The geometry tests check unit radii, matching cube-panel boundary nodes,
icosahedral edge incidence and valence, Euler's identity, and total spherical
triangle area 4π. A deterministic equal-area sample checks Yin–Yang coverage
and overlap; this sampled check is not a formal coverage proof. Reproduce both
figures with python scripts/build_spherical_meshes.py; the
geometry manifest records construction choices,
area statistics and source/artifact hashes. These checks do not establish
transport accuracy, seam conservation or geophysical wave convergence. Useful
