## Site coverage and counting rules — Biological model survey# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/site-coverage/#biological-model-survey
Coverage: reading

Logistic population growth — Reading only. The linked original is the later 1847 memoir; the 1838 note itself was not audited. The differential equation is not the discrete logistic map.
Michaelis–Menten and full enzyme kinetics — Reading only. The 1913 rapid-equilibrium interpretation and the 1925 quasi-steady-state derivation must remain distinct.
Lotka–Volterra predator–prey — Reading only.
McKendrick age-structured population — Reading only. This is the classical age-transport form; the later von Foerster lineage is acknowledged without treating its date as the first appearance.
SIR and SEIR compartment models — Reading only. The original general epidemic framework is broader than this SIR specialization. Population-count and fraction conventions give different β definitions.
Fisher–KPP invasion front — Reading only. Fisher–KPP is a conventional family name; the independent KPP 1937 original remains an archival follow-up. The exact special speed is not the minimal speed.
Monod growth and chemostat — Reading only. This writes one constant-yield extension of saturation growth, not a universal metabolic model.
Hodgkin–Huxley membrane dynamics — Reading only. The original squid-axon model is not a calibrated human cardiac model. No single rate parameter set is selected by this survey.

## Site coverage and counting rules — Biological model survey# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/site-coverage/#biological-model-survey
Coverage: reading

Turing reaction–diffusion framework — Reading only. A spot image or unequal diffusion coefficients alone do not establish a Turing mechanism. Boundary conditions determine the available modes.
FitzHugh–Nagumo excitation and recovery — Reading only. This is a common normalized variant; cubic coefficients, recovery signs and nondimensionalization differ between formulations.
Keller–Segel chemotaxis — Reading only. This is a common two-field reduction of a more detailed original formulation. Blowup thresholds depend on dimension, domain, boundary and chemical dynamics.
Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor — Reading only. Source densities, saturation and baseline production vary across the model family. This simplified formula is not a verbatim transcription of every original variant.
Fluid–elastic structure and immersed boundaries — Reading only. Immersed boundary is a numerical coupling method, not itself a closed biological constitutive equation. The existing periodic MAC solver does not implement this coupling.
Chemical master equation and Gillespie SSA — Reading only. The 1977 paper is a foundational SSA reference, not a priority claim for all master equations. SSA is a solver; the reaction network is the model. A seed documents a trajectory, not an ensemble validation.

## Site coverage and counting rules — Biological model survey# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/site-coverage/#biological-model-survey
Coverage: reading

Mackey–Glass delayed physiological feedback — Reading only. A scalar initial value alone is insufficient. The delayed ODE is distinct from a spatial reaction–diffusion model.
Replicator evolutionary game dynamics — Reading only. No universal Lyapunov function or equivalence of fixed point and evolutionarily stable strategy is assumed.
Schnakenberg reaction–diffusion — Reading only. A mathematical chemical pattern model; matching a visual biological pattern does not calibrate it to a tissue.
Shigesada–Kawasaki–Teramoto cross-diffusion — Reading only. The displayed homogeneous-environment reduction omits the original environmental-potential terms. It is not equivalent to two independent scalar diffusion equations.
Gray–Scott spatial autocatalysis — Reading only. 1983 is the well-mixed CSTR source; Pearson 1993 is the spatial pattern reference. Spot division does not by itself demonstrate cell division or a linear Turing instability.
Aliev–Panfilov cardiac excitation — Reading only. Monodomain/bidomain tissue models add conductivity tensors and, for bidomain, an extracellular elliptic constraint. They are not automatically included by this two-variable model.
Repressilator mRNA–protein network — Reading only. The six-variable form is distinct from a reduced three-protein oscillator; oscillations are parameter-dependent.

## Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald — Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/slab-ewald/
Coverage: reading

Interfaces often require periodicity in two directions and isolation in the normal direction. Elongating a triply periodic cell is not identical to evaluating the genuinely two-periodic Green function.

## Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/slab-ewald/#model
Coverage: reading

For a neutral cell of volume V, normal z and unit Coulomb prefactor, the Yeh–Berkowitz correction adds a dipole contribution to a specified three-periodic Ewald baseline. Its coordinate derivative gives the normal force correction. The formula assumes neutrality and a conducting-boundary 3D reference.
M_z=\sum_iq_i z_i,\qquad \Delta E=\frac{2\pi}{V}M_z^2,\qquad \Delta F_{i,z}=-\frac{4\pi}{V}q_iM_z.

## Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/slab-ewald/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Place slabs in an elongated cell with vacuum, converge the 3D sums, and add the dipole correction. Increase the vacuum height to assess residual image interactions. At finite vacuum height, this is not a claim of exact equivalence to a fully two-periodic summation.

## Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/slab-ewald/#conditions
Coverage: reading

Charged slabs, other external dielectric conditions, electrodes and imposed fields require additional formulations. Keep self and k=0 conventions distinct from this correction. Neutral-cell M_z is invariant under an origin shift; net charge destroys that property.

## Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/slab-ewald/#verification
Coverage: reading

Use neutral charge pairs or a dipole layer and vary vacuum height independently of reciprocal/mesh cutoffs. Compare with an independent two-periodic reference when available, and finite-difference the energy for normal forces. Agreement with an uncorrected 3D calculation cannot establish zero slab error.

## Sparse and nonlinear systems: measure the actual residual — 1986–1992: nonsymmetric Krylov methods# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/sparse-nonlinear/#19861992-nonsymmetric-krylov-methods
Coverage: reading

Saad–Schultz (1986) introduces GMRES;
van der Vorst (1992) introduces BiCGSTAB.
The implemented GMRES uses Arnoldi reorthogonalization and small Hessenberg
least squares, restarting after a specified number of inner iterations.
BiCGSTAB has explicit breakdown reporting; it need not have monotone residuals.
Both implementations apply a fixed right preconditioner:
A M^{-1} z=b,\qquad x=M^{-1}z,
\qquad \|b-Ax\|_2\leq\max(\mathrm{atol},\mathrm{rtol}\|b\|_2).
The stopping history recomputes the true residual. Jacobi uses diagonal
scaling. ILU(0) retains the supplied nonzero structure, with no fill, pivoting
or reordering; tiny pivots raise an explicit failure. This is not a robust
replacement for a production sparse factorization.

## Sparse and nonlinear systems: measure the actual residual — Newton and conditioning# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/sparse-nonlinear/#newton-and-conditioning
Coverage: reading

Newton solves J(x)δ=−F(x), then chooses a backtracked step length with an
Armijo residual decrease. The Newton–Krylov demonstration assembles J and
uses GMRES; it is not matrix free. Bratu's equation is checked against an
analytic solution at two spatial resolutions, including inner-solve failures.
A small residual is not automatically a small solution error:
\frac{\|x-\hat x\|}{\|x\|}
\leq \kappa(A)\frac{\|b-A\hat x\|}{\|b\|}.
Condition number, eigenvalue distribution and nonnormality describe different
features. A smaller condition number alone does not rank restarted GMRES.
CG still requires an SPD operator and suitable SPD preconditioning; generic
ILU(0) is not asserted to satisfy that requirement.
The nonsymmetric example is first-order upwind advection plus centered diffusion
with zero Dirichlet data. Iteration counts have different per-iteration costs;
the figure makes no wall-clock ranking. See the data and source hashes,
FEM assembly, and implicit ODE stages.

## Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson — Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spectral-element/
Coverage: reading

The spectral element method (SEM) partitions a domain into elements and approximates the field with high-degree local polynomials. It connects finite-element assembly with high-order approximation of smooth functions. This chapter adopts a continuous Galerkin Legendre GLL variant and a small reproducible two-dimensional Poisson problem.

## Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson — Connect high-order local polynomials [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spectral-element/#local-polynomials
Coverage: reading

u_h|_{K_e}(\xi,\eta)=\sum_{i,j=0}^{p}U^e_{ij}\ell_i(\xi)\ell_j(\eta),\qquad u_h\in C^0(\Omega)
Map each square to reference coordinates in [−1,1]². Shared boundary degrees of freedom assemble a C0 field, without imposing continuous derivatives. SEM belongs to the high-order finite-element family; finite elements in general are not restricted to linear elements. Element-local polynomials also differ from a single global Fourier expansion.

## Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson — Start from the Poisson weak form [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spectral-element/#weak-form
Coverage: reading

\int_\Omega\nabla v_h\cdot\nabla u_h\,d\Omega=\int_\Omega v_h f\,d\Omega,\qquad v_h|_{\partial\Omega}=0
Multiply −Laplacian u=f by a test function and integrate by parts, transferring one derivative to each factor. Zero Dirichlet tests remove the boundary term. This implementation approximates the integrals with GLL quadrature for constant coefficients and affine squares.

## Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson — GLL nodes, quadrature and matrices [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spectral-element/#gll
Coverage: reading

(1-\xi_i^2)P_p^\prime(\xi_i)=0,\qquad w_i=\frac{2}{p(p+1)P_p(\xi_i)^2},\qquad i=0,\ldots,pD_{ij}=\ell_j^\prime(\xi_i),\quad W=\operatorname{diag}(w_i),\quad S=D^TWD,\quad K_e=\frac{h_y}{h_x}S\otimes W+\frac{h_x}{h_y}W\otimes Sb^e_{ij}=\frac{h_xh_y}{4}w_iw_jf(x_{e,i},y_{e,j}),\qquad KU=b
The p+1 GLL nodes are the roots of the derivative of the degree-p Legendre polynomial plus both endpoints. The one-dimensional quadrature is exact through degree 2p−1. Nodal interpolation makes the quadrature mass diagonal, not exactly integrated for every degree-2p product. Two-dimensional stiffness also contains transverse products, so the quadrature convention matters. Assemble local tensor-product stiffness/load contributions, eliminate the boundary values and solve the sparse system.

Coverage: reading

AspectPublished P1 FEMThis GLL-SEM

## Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson — Small example:2D Poisson h/p refinement [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spectral-element/#example
Coverage: reading

\Omega=(0,1)^2,\quad u_*=\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y),\quad f=2\pi^2u_*,\quad u|_{\partial\Omega}=0
At p=2, use 2/4/8 SEM elements per coordinate and 4/8/16 subdivisions for the existing triangular P1 FEM. Both have 9/49/225 free unknowns. Separately fix 2 x 2 elements and vary p=1..6. The comparison executes byte-identical modules from the published Numart distribution; that historical release remains unchanged.
Actual saved fields and measurements. A nodal-error picture is distinct from an error norm integrated over element interiors.

## Spectral elements: high-order finite elements and 2D Poisson — Distinguish residual, continuous error and observed order [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spectral-element/#error-and-refinement
Coverage: reading

E_{L^2}=\left[\int_\Omega(u_h-u_*)^2\,d\Omega\right]^{1/2},\quad E_{H^1}=\left[\int_\Omega|\nabla u_h-\nabla u_*|^2\,d\Omega\right]^{1/2}E_{L^2}\sim h^{p+1},\qquad E_{H^1}\sim h^p\quad\text{(smooth solution and resolved quadrature)}
Integrate errors at separate higher-order Gauss points, not only at GLL nodes. A small linear-system residual alone does not imply a small continuous-PDE error. On the last h refinement, p2 SEM gives L2 order about 3.04 and H1-seminorm order 2.01; P1 FEM gives 1.97 and 0.99. At 225 free unknowns, L2 errors are about 2.49e−4 for SEM and 5.38e−3 for P1. At p6 on 2 x 2 elements, L2 error is about 3.78e−7.
These observations depend on smoothness, boundaries, element geometry, quadrature and solver choices. They establish neither universal p convergence near singularities nor a speed/accuracy ranking for all problems. Curved elements, mixed velocity/pressure spaces and fluid coupling are outside this execution.

## Spline interpolation — Spline interpolation [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/splines/
Coverage: reading

Splines join piecewise low-degree polynomials with specified continuity. Distinguish them from a single global high-degree polynomial and distinguish exact interpolation from smoothing noisy data.

## Spline interpolation — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/splines/#model
Coverage: reading

Use a nondecreasing knot sequence tᵢ and degree p. Nᵢ,₀ is the indicator of [tᵢ,tᵢ₊₁); zero-denominator terms in the recursion are defined as zero. Degree p means order p+1.
N_{i,p}(x)=\frac{x-t_i}{t_{i+p}-t_i}N_{i,p-1}(x)+\frac{t_{i+p+1}-x}{t_{i+p+1}-t_{i+1}}N_{i+1,p-1}(x),\qquad s(x)=\sum_i c_iN_{i,p}(x).

## Spline interpolation — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/splines/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Represent s=ΣcᵢNᵢ,ₚ and determine coefficients by interpolation or least squares. A natural cubic spline sets endpoint second derivatives to zero; clamped conditions prescribe endpoint first derivatives. Determining coefficients and evaluating the spline by de Boor’s algorithm are separate stages.

## Spline interpolation — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/splines/#conditions
Coverage: reading

An interior knot of multiplicity r generally gives Cᵖ⁻ʳ continuity. Cubic splines do not automatically preserve monotonicity or positivity and can overshoot. Extrapolation depends on the chosen endpoint convention and is not covered by an in-interval interpolation argument.

## Spline interpolation — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/splines/#verification
Coverage: reading

Check polynomial reproduction, one-sided derivatives at knots and endpoint conditions. For noiseless functions study refinement; for noisy data separately report held-out prediction errors and smoothing-parameter dependence.

## Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME — Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spme/
Coverage: reading

SPME approximates Ewald structure factors using smooth cardinal B-splines. Treat it as a specific interpolation-and-force construction rather than a synonym for every PME implementation.

## Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME — Problem and representative equations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spme/#model
Coverage: reading

Let uᵢ be particle coordinates in mesh units and Mₚ a cardinal B-spline of order p, not degree p. The product below is the local tensor assignment in three dimensions. Fourier structure factors require a correction for the spline response.
Q_{m_xm_ym_z}=\sum_iq_i\prod_{d\in\{x,y,z\}}M_p(u_{id}-m_d),\qquad \deg M_p=p-1.

## Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME — Algorithm [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spme/#algorithm
Coverage: reading

Spread charge over p neighboring mesh points in each direction, evaluate a corrected reciprocal mesh energy by FFT, and obtain forces using derivatives of the assignment in analytical differentiation. Record the spline order and mesh together with whether differentiation is analytical or in Fourier space.

## Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME — Conditions and pitfalls [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spme/#conditions
Coverage: reading

Smooth assignment alone does not guarantee both energy consistency and exact net-force cancellation. Ewald neutrality, boundary and self-term conventions still apply. Comparisons with original PME should control error tolerance and differentiation rules, not merely the number of mesh points.
The companion also uses analytical energy gradients with B-spline orders 4/6. Discrete energy–force consistency, common-translation mesh effects and net force are separate observables. Finite-mesh aliasing generally permits nonzero net force; exact momentum conservation is not claimed.

## Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME — What to check [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/spme/#verification
Coverage: reading

Measure force errors against the same converged Ewald reference and check energy finite differences. Report common-translation mesh effects and total force separately. Ensure real-space truncation is not hiding the reciprocal-space convergence trend.
The design compares 16³/24³/40³ meshes and several common translations against matching direct-Ewald and independent theta references. It separates partition of unity/charge, energy differences, RMS/maximum force errors and real-space truncation; it supplies no evidence for long MD or original PME.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — Choose space and time discretizations separately# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#choose-space-and-time-discretizations-separately
Coverage: reading

Forward, backward, and centered spatial differences are
D_+u_j=\frac{u_{j+1}-u_j}{h},\qquad
D_-u_j=\frac{u_j-u_{j-1}}h,\qquad
D_0u_j=\frac{u_{j+1}-u_{j-1}}{2h}.
For smooth functions, the first two are first-order accurate and the centered
stencil is second order. Compare them with numart.advection.finite_difference.
For linear advection u_t+a u_x=0, upwinding follows information propagation:
use a backward difference for a>0 and a forward difference for a<0.
A forward difference is therefore not synonymous with an upwind difference.
Forward Euler in time gives u^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^n; backward Euler gives
u^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^{n+1} and requires a system solve. A backward spatial
stencil alone does not make a method implicit.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — CFL: can the stencil reach the information it needs?# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#cfl-can-the-stencil-reach-the-information-it-needs
Coverage: reading

For constant-coefficient periodic advection with an explicit nearest-neighbor
stencil, domain-of-dependence reasoning requires |a|Δt/h ≤ 1. The constant
changes with the stencil, Runge–Kutta method, DG degree, and dimension.
Explicit diffusion introduces a Δt=O(h²) restriction. A CFL condition is
generally necessary rather than sufficient for stability.
Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (1928).
Forward-time, centered-space (FTCS) advection is a counterexample. Substituting
a Fourier mode u_j^n=G^n e^{ijθ} gives
G=1-i C\sin θ,\quad |G|^2=1+C^2\sin^2 θ,
\qquad C=a\Delta t/h.
Some modes grow even when |C|<1. The scheme is unstable under ordinary
fixed-CFL grid refinement.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — Lax–Friedrichs and Lax–Wendroff# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#laxfriedrichs-and-laxwendroff
Coverage: reading

The classical Lax–Friedrichs scheme is
u_j^{n+1}=\tfrac12(u_{j+1}^n+u_{j-1}^n)
-\tfrac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n),\qquad
G=\cos θ-iC\sin θ.
Since |G|²=1-(1-C²)sin²θ, periodic linear advection is stable for |C|≤1.
Classical LF uses the numerical-viscosity coefficient h/Δt. Rusanov uses a
local maximum wave speed; WENO here uses global LF flux splitting. These are
different discrete constructions.
Lax (1954).
Lax–Wendroff is
u_j^{n+1}=u_j^n-\tfrac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n)
+\tfrac{C^2}{2}(u_{j+1}^n-2u_j^n+u_{j-1}^n),
G=1-iC\sin θ+C^2(\cos θ-1),\quad
|G|^2=1-4C^2(1-C^2)\sin^4(θ/2).
Its stability condition for this problem is also |C|≤1. Second-order accuracy
does not itself suppress oscillations near discontinuities.
Lax–Wendroff (1960).
Tests compare the analytical amplification factors from amplification with
actual mode evolution from difference_step. The gallery seeds a small
Nyquist perturbation and compares C=0.8 with C=1.1.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — Dissipation and dispersion: read amplitude and phase separately# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#dissipation-and-dispersion
Coverage: reading

The same amplification factor used to test growth also explains two distinct errors: numerical dissipation damps a wave's amplitude; numerical dispersion changes its propagation speed in a wavelength-dependent way. Consider constant-speed scalar advection on a periodic uniform grid. Let h be the grid spacing, Δt the positive time step, k the wavenumber, θ the dimensionless grid wavenumber, and C the signed Courant number. The Fourier convention and exact one-step factor are
\begin{gathered}u_t+a u_x=0,\qquad x_j=jh,\quad\theta=kh,\quad C=\frac{a\Delta t}{h},\\u_j^n=\widehat u^{\,n}e^{ij\theta},\qquad G_{\rm exact}=e^{-ia k\Delta t}=e^{-iC\theta}.\end{gathered}
The exact solution translates without changing amplitude. This makes the model useful for separating artificial damping from transport error.

Here, “no dissipation preserves amplitude” means preserving the magnitude of each Fourier component. Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#waveform-evolution

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — What the amplification factor measures# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#vn-amplitude-and-phase
Coverage: reading

For a linear, translation-invariant one-step scheme, write its factor in polar form:
\begin{aligned}G(\theta)&=|G(\theta)|e^{-i\phi(\theta)},\\\widehat u^{\,n}&=G(\theta)^n\widehat u^{\,0},\qquad\frac{|\widehat u^{\,n}|}{|\widehat u^{\,0}|}=|G(\theta)|^n.\end{aligned}
Thus |G|<1 damps this mode; repeated steps accumulate the loss. |G|=1 preserves its amplitude, while |G|>1 amplifies it. For this scalar periodic problem, the familiar requirement |G|≤1 controls growth, but says nothing about whether the amplitude stays close to its exact value of one.
For 0<|G|, the loss can also be expressed as a damping rate σnum per unit time:
\begin{aligned}\sigma_{\rm num}&=-\frac{\log|G|}{\Delta t},\\|\widehat u^{\,n}|&=e^{-\sigma_{\rm num}t_n}|\widehat u^{\,0}|,\qquad t_n=n\Delta t.\end{aligned}
This is a decay rate with units of inverse time, not a diffusion coefficient. At G=0 the mode vanishes in one step; a finite damping rate and phase are undefined.
Phase needs a sign convention as well. Use arg₀ for an argument continued from G(0)=1 along a branch on which G never vanishes. The minus sign matches the exact factor above:
\begin{aligned}\phi(\theta)&=-\arg_0G(\theta),\qquad\omega_{\rm num}=\frac{\phi(\theta)}{\Delta t},\\\frac{c_{\rm num}}a&=\frac{\omega_{\rm num}/k}a=\frac{\phi(\theta)}{C\theta}\qquad(ak\ne0).\end{aligned}

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — What the amplification factor measures# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#vn-amplitude-and-phase
Coverage: reading

Correct transport requires φ=Cθ, as well as |G|=1. A stable wave can travel at the wrong speed and accumulate a large position error. At θ=0, use the low-wavenumber limit for the speed ratio. At G=0 the scheme has removed the mode and its phase is undefined. Principal arguments wrap by 2π; treating that jump as a physical change gives a false dispersion curve. At the Nyquist endpoints θ=±π, the sampled modes coincide, so their propagation direction cannot be uniquely recovered from grid samples.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — Three examples reveal different errors# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#vn-three-discretizations
Coverage: reading

For a>0, forward Euler with backward spatial differencing is the first-order upwind scheme. Direct substitution gives
\begin{aligned}G_{\rm up}&=1-C(1-e^{-i\theta}),\\|G_{\rm up}|^2&=1-4C(1-C)\sin^2\!\left(\frac\theta2\right),\\&\hspace{1em}0\le C\le1\qquad(a>0).\end{aligned}
For 0<C<1, every nonconstant resolved Fourier mode is damped. This is numerical dissipation: the underlying advection equation has no physical decay. Its phase generally also differs from Cθ. For a<0, reverse the upwind stencil.
Centered differencing with time still continuous instead gives
\begin{aligned}\frac{d u_j}{dt}&=-a\frac{u_{j+1}-u_{j-1}}{2h},\qquad\lambda_h=-i\frac ah\sin\theta,\\\omega_h&=\frac ah\sin\theta,\qquad\frac{c_h}a=\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}.\end{aligned}
The eigenvalue is purely imaginary, so this semidiscrete mode has no amplitude decay. Yet sinθ/θ differs from one: it is dispersive. For θ=π/2, the phase speed is only 2/π≈0.637 times a. At θ=π the centered derivative vanishes, a stationary Nyquist checkerboard annihilated by the centered derivative, rather than correct transport.
Time discretization changes the result. With forward Euler,
\begin{aligned}G_{\rm FE+centered}&=1-iC\sin\theta,\\|G_{\rm FE+centered}|^2&=1+C^2\sin^2\theta.\end{aligned}

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — Three examples reveal different errors# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#vn-three-discretizations
Coverage: reading

Modes with sinθ≠0 grow for any nonzero C, explaining the FTCS instability discussed above. Other time integrators have different amplitude and phase responses on the same spatial eigenvalues. The linearized centered-wave discussion in KEEP and its RK4 amplitude and phase analysis make this separation explicit.
For Lax–Wendroff (1960), the factor already derived above also yields
\begin{aligned}G_{\rm LW}&=1-iC\sin\theta+C^2(\cos\theta-1),\\|G_{\rm LW}|^2&=1-4C^2(1-C^2)\sin^4\!\left(\frac\theta2\right).\end{aligned}
At generic 0<|C|<1 it therefore has amplitude error as well as phase error; calling it “purely dispersive” is incorrect. Its leading smooth-wave error can be dispersive without eliminating higher-order damping. At C=1, both upwind and Lax–Wendroff reduce to G=e−iθ, an exact one-cell shift on this grid. This special Courant number is not representative of other step sizes.
For C=0.8 and θ=π/2 (four grid spacings per wavelength), the one-step amplitude gain is about 0.8246 for upwind and 0.8773 for Lax–Wendroff. Their phase-speed ratios are about 1.0551 and 0.9135, respectively: the first travels too fast and the second too slowly. Both are stable, yet both have amplitude and phase errors.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — Keep the physical and numerical questions distinct# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#vn-interpreting-stability
Coverage: reading

If the physical PDE includes viscosity or another decay mechanism, the exact |G| can itself be below one for the mode considered; compare numerical damping with that exact decay. Likewise, a physically dispersive PDE has a wavenumber-dependent exact phase speed. Error means disagreement with the physical reference.
A-stability and L-stability classify a time integrator's response to linear test modes; neither guarantees accurate wave propagation at a chosen resolution. The formulas here concern scalar periodic linear advection. They do not certify nonlinear Euler dynamics, shocks, or wall boundary treatments.
A useful diagnostic first fixes h and reduces Δt to expose the time integrator's contribution. Then reduce h with temporal error controlled. Refining with C held fixed changes both scales and does not by itself separate the two errors. For a smooth single mode, compare amplitude and unwrapped phase at the same physical time; agreement in only one of these quantities is incomplete evidence of accuracy.
The formulas and worked values here follow by directly substituting Fourier modes into the displayed differences. For the assumptions of the analysis and comparison against the exact amplification factor, see R. R. Rosales’s author lecture notes (2022), §1 and §1.1.2.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — The Lax–Richtmyer equivalence theorem# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#the-laxrichtmyer-equivalence-theorem
Coverage: reading

Consider a well-posed linear initial-value problem in an appropriate Banach
space and a consistent linear difference approximation. When stability
means uniform boundedness of the discrete evolution operators over a fixed
finite time interval, stability is equivalent to convergence.
Lax–Richtmyer (1956), original paper.
Writing the error as e^{n+1}=S_h e^n+Δt τ^n, the bound ||S_h^m||≤M_T gives
||e^n||≤M_T||e^0||+M_T T max||τ^k||. Consistency makes the truncation-error
term tend to zero, providing the basic stability-to-convergence argument.
The converse requires a uniform-boundedness argument.
The theorem does not directly certify nonlinear Euler, WENO, shocks, or
arbitrary boundary treatments. The Fourier criterion |G|≤1 used here applies
to periodic, constant-coefficient scalar problems. Boundaries, variable
coefficients, nonnormal matrices, and multistep schemes need additional analysis.

## Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax — Time steps in the first edition# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stability/#time-steps-in-the-first-edition
Coverage: reading

Euler and barotropic systems: Δt=C h/max(|u|+c), with default C=0.3.
DG: Δt=C h/((2p+1)|a|), with default C=0.2.
2D MHD: Δt=C/[max(s_x)/h+max(s_y)/h], with default C=0.3.
These conservative choices are checked on selected examples. They are not
rigorous nonlinear stability limits for every initial condition.

## Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions — Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/steady-runge-kutta/
Coverage: reading

Interpret multistage pseudo-time iterations as smoothers for a steady residual. A Jameson–Schmidt–Turkel-family example connects stage coefficients, stability polynomials, nonlinear order, high-frequency damping and preconditioning.

## Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions — The target is R(U)=0, not a physical-time trajectory [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/steady-runge-kutta/#steady-residual
Coverage: reading

For a discrete steady Euler/Navier–Stokes residual R, iterate an artificial ODE in pseudo time τ toward its root. Here R is the conservative residual divided by cell volume. The step is a pseudo-time step; the aim is an adequately converged residual and steady observables, not an accurate physical transient.
The following base-state recurrence forms every stage from the same U^(0), unlike chaining forward-Euler increments from the preceding stage. Compare coefficients only after matching residual sign, cell-volume scaling and any preconditioning action.
\frac{dU}{d\tau}=-R(U),\quad U^{(0)}=U^n,\quad U^{(k)}=U^{(0)}-\alpha_k\Delta\tau R(U^{(k-1)}),\quad U^{n+1}=U^{(s)}.

## Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions — A representative Jameson-family four-stage iteration [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/steady-runge-kutta/#jameson-four-stage
Coverage: reading

Consider these coefficients with the same autonomous residual reevaluated at every stage. For R(U)=AU, the stability polynomial equals classical RK4. The simplified recurrence is not a complete specification of the original fluxes, artificial dissipation and dissipation-update schedule.
Equality of linear stability polynomials does not establish nonlinear fourth-order physical-time accuracy. This base-state recurrence is generally second order for nonlinear autonomous ODEs: it fails the third-order condition bᵀ(c⊙c)=1/3. Distinguish its steady-solver purpose and nonlinear order conditions from classical RK4.
(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\alpha_4)=(1/4,1/3,1/2,1),\qquad z=-\Delta\tau\lambda,\quad \mathcal R_4(z)=1+z+z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24.b^Tc=\tfrac12,\qquad b^T(c\odot c)=\tfrac14\ne\tfrac13\quad\text{for the stated base-state four-stage recurrence}.

## Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions — Stability and high-frequency damping are different [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/steady-runge-kutta/#high-frequency-damping
Coverage: reading

For linearized residual modes, the iteration multiplier is a stability polynomial. |ℛ|≤1 prevents growth, but |ℛ| near one barely damps error. A multigrid smoother seeks small maximum amplification μ on frequencies H not representable on the coarse grid.
For a purely decaying z=−2 mode, this four-stage polynomial gives ℛ=1/3, while near-zero low-frequency modes decay slowly. Pushing the step to a stability boundary does not maximize damping or minimize time to convergence. Advection and diffusion occupy different spectral regions.
e^{n+1}=\mathcal R_s(-\Delta\tau A)e^n,\qquad\mu=\max_{\theta\in\mathcal H}\left|\mathcal R_s(-\Delta\tau\lambda_h(\theta))\right|.

## Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions — Residual smoothing, preconditioning and multigrid [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/steady-runge-kutta/#smoothing-preconditioning
Coverage: reading

Residual smoothing is a separate spatial filtering operation, not the choice of RK stage coefficients. With dimensionless centered D₂ on a uniform periodic grid and ε≥0, the example below attenuates high-frequency residuals. An invertible filter retains the residual root but changes the iteration spectrum.
Low-Mach preconditioning changes acoustic/convective scales, local stepping changes per-cell iteration increments, and coarse correction treats errors poorly reduced by the smoother. Combined iterations still require boundary/variable-coefficient/nonnormality analysis and must be distinguished from physical-time integration.
(I-\varepsilon D_2)\overline r=r,\qquad \widehat D_2(\theta)=-4\sin^2(\theta/2),\quad \widehat{\overline r}(\theta)=\frac{\widehat r(\theta)}{1+4\varepsilon\sin^2(\theta/2)}.

## Damping Runge–Kutta iterations for steady solutions — Measure residuals, steady observables and work [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/steady-runge-kutta/#verification
Coverage: reading

Measure Fourier-mode damping on a manufactured Poisson-type problem and compare with μ. For compressible flow track true residuals scaled by conservative component and steady quantities such as forces, mass flow and conservation balances. When smoothing residuals, also display the original unsmoothed residual.
Report residual evaluations and linear-solve work, final errors and termination reasons, not only stage/cycle counts. Compare methods at the same steady solution and tolerance. This chapter supplies algorithmic reading, not a dedicated Jameson solver or new flow-validation results.

## Stiff integration: solve the stage, control the time error — Implicit stages and stability# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stiff-integration/#implicit-stages-and-stability
Coverage: reading

Backward Euler solves y_new−y_old−h f(t_new,y_new)=0. BDF2 solves
\frac{3y_{n+1}-4y_n+y_{n-1}}{2h}=f(t_{n+1},y_{n+1}).
Alexander (1977) is the source for the
L-stable, two-stage, second-order singly diagonally implicit family used here:
\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2,\qquad
A=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma&0\\1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},
\quad b=(1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(\gamma,1).
Each diagonal stage is a separate nonlinear solve. An implicit method can
permit steps beyond an explicit stability limit, while accuracy still limits
useful step size. A converged Newton residual measures the stage equation,
not the temporal discretization error.

## Stiff integration: solve the stage, control the time error — Adaptive and split steps# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/stiff-integration/#adaptive-and-split-steps
Coverage: reading

The adaptive implementation compares one full SDIRK2 step with two half steps.
The local error estimate is (y_half−y_full)/3, scaled by
atol+rtol max(|y_old|,|y_half|). It accepts the two-half-step value, without
Richardson extrapolation, and adjusts h with exponent −1/3. Rejected trials
and accepted steps are counted; reaching a trial limit raises an error.
IMEX Euler evaluates one part explicitly and the other implicitly. This
minimal first-order split is not the higher-order IMEX RK constructions of
Ascher–Ruuth–Spiteri (1997).
The explicit part retains its own stability restriction. Variable-step BDF,
embedded DIRK pairs and operator splitting remain extensions.
The stiff test y′=−1000(y−cos t)−sin t has exact solution cos t when y(0)=1.
The manifest records maximum errors at actual
integration nodes and adaptive step counts. Separate tests verify order on a
nonlinear, nonautonomous ODE and strong damping of a stiff decay mode.
The coarse stiff-forced refinement is not in a uniform second-order regime.
BDF2 startup and stiff order reduction affect the maximum-over-nodes error;
the nonlinear nonstiff order test checks the formal temporal order separately.
For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms,
see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/
Coverage: reading

A symplectic integrator advances a Hamiltonian system while preserving its canonical two-form. This is the map property behind the good long-time behavior of many orbital and particle integrators. It does not generally preserve the original Hamiltonian exactly. The Hamiltonian map notebook separates those two questions with computed examples.
THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — What the map preserves# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/#what-the-map-preserves
Coverage: reading

For state z = (q,p), Hamilton’s equations and the symplectic condition are
\dot z=J\nabla H(z),\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad D\Phi_h(z)^T J D\Phi_h(z)=J.
The last identity says that each numerical step is a canonical transformation. For one degree of freedom it is equivalent to det(D Phi) = 1, preserving oriented phase-plane area. In higher dimensions, preservation of total volume alone is weaker than symplecticity.
Three separate properties should be tested: preservation of the two-form, preservation of H, and time symmetry Phi_(−h) = Phi_h^(−1). Symplectic Euler already illustrates the distinction: it is symplectic but is neither exactly energy preserving nor time symmetric in general.

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — Split the Hamiltonian, compose exact subflows# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/#split-the-hamiltonian-compose-exact-subflows
Coverage: reading

For a unit-mass separable system H(q,p) = p²/2 + V(q), the two subflows are a drift and a kick:
D_h(q,p)=(q+hp,p),\qquad K_h(q,p)=(q,p-h\nabla V(q)).
Each is symplectic; compositions remain symplectic. The notebook includes kick–drift symplectic Euler, and the symmetric second-order Störmer–Verlet update
p_{n+1/2}=p_n-\frac h2\nabla V(q_n),\quad
q_{n+1}=q_n+h p_{n+1/2},\quad
p_{n+1}=p_{n+1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(q_{n+1}).
This is the mechanical Leapfrog/velocity-Verlet formulation. It differs from the two-step scalar recurrence in the earlier time-integration notebook.

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — Fourth order by composition# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/#fourth-order-by-composition
Coverage: reading

Writing S2(h) for a Verlet step, one fourth-order composition is
S_4(h)=S_2(a h)\,S_2(b h)\,S_2(a h),\qquad
a=\frac1{2-2^{1/3}},\quad b=-\frac{2^{1/3}}{2-2^{1/3}}.
Yoshida (1990) develops higher-order symplectic compositions. Here b is negative: an internal substep goes backward in time. The construction is suitable for the smooth conservative examples used here; simply applying it to irreversible diffusion, shocks, or collision handling is not justified. Higher order also does not establish unconditional stability or an equal-cost advantage.

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — Energy and a modified Hamiltonian# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/#energy-and-a-modified-hamiltonian
Coverage: reading

Backward error analysis describes a nearby, generally formal modified Hamiltonian. Under smoothness, bounded-trajectory, small-step, and related hypotheses, this explains small long-time energy errors. It does not assert an exact invariant of the original H for every orbit or step size. Hairer, Lubich, and Wanner (2003) develop this geometric viewpoint and its assumptions.
For the special oscillator H = (p²+q²)/2, kick–drift–kick Verlet preserves the quadratic invariant
I_h=\frac12p^2+\frac12\left(1-\frac{h^2}{4}\right)q^2
up to roundoff. H itself oscillates. This invariant is not a claim that its unscaled Hamiltonian flow is exactly the numerical time-h map. The oscillator map is bounded for |h| < 2; above that limit it can be symplectic and unstable.

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — Implicit midpoint and RK4 as comparisons# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/#implicit-midpoint-and-rk4-as-comparisons
Coverage: reading

Implicit midpoint is symplectic and time symmetric when its endpoint equation is solved accurately. It preserves the quadratic oscillator H to roundoff here. It need not exactly conserve a nonquadratic H. Classical RK4 is fourth order but is generally neither symplectic nor time symmetric. Good short-time accuracy alone does not certify the map’s geometry.
The second test problem is H = p²/2 + q²/2 + q⁴/4, a smooth nonlinear oscillator. It makes midpoint’s special quadratic-energy conservation visibly distinguishable from a general claim.

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — Reproducible notebook and checks# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/#reproducible-notebook-and-checks
Coverage: reading

from numart.hamiltonian import trajectory, energy, canonical_step, J
t, z = trajectory(h=0.2, steps=1000, method='yoshida4', system='quartic')
print(max(abs((energy(z, 'quartic')-energy(z[0], 'quartic'))/energy(z[0], 'quartic'))))
_, M = canonical_step([0.7, 0.4], 0.2, 'yoshida4', 'quartic', True)
print(M.T @ J @ M - J)
The computed dataset and source manifest supplies 30 Python trajectories: five methods, two Hamiltonians, and h = 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4, all to T = 200 from (q,p) = (1,0.2). Plotted trajectories contain at most 1001 samples; maximum energy errors use every integration step. The phase-patch view applies one step to a square centered at (0.7,0.4). Its sampled polygon boundary is an illustration; the displayed local defect uses an analytic map Jacobian at the patch center.
Tests check refinement orders against the exact oscillator, analytic Jacobians against independent finite differences, the canonical identity on both potentials, time reversal for symmetric methods, the Verlet quadratic invariant, and the difference between quadratic and nonquadratic midpoint energy. The gallery and notebook are educational fixed-step examples, not orbit-accuracy or timing rankings.

## Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise — Connecting to particle gravity# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/symplectic/#connecting-to-particle-gravity
Coverage: reading

A fixed step and a force that is the gradient of a consistent position-dependent potential support the splitting argument. A generic approximate Tree force, changing opening decisions, ad hoc mesh interpolation, or state-dependent step selection does not automatically retain that proof. Force approximation and time integration need joint tests. Continue with particle gravity and Poisson solvers and gravity boundary kernels.
An operator-splitting reading now compares first-order Lie–Trotter and second-order Strang with a small exact-flow illustration. It does not add a general splitting implementation to this chapter’s existing solver package. A lightweight fixed-input example now runs both on the same reaction–diffusion problem.

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — Thermostats: temperature control and distributions [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/
Coverage: reading

Compare fluctuations, ergodicity and time correlations as well as mean temperature, from Nosé–Hoover and velocity rescaling to stochastic and momentum-conserving methods.
Retain the earlier two-method comparison of Langevin and CSVR. Preserve the earlier one-degree-of-freedom harmonic Langevin/BAOAB case. A separate edition compares both baths with the same OBABO splitting for a nondegenerate two-degree harmonic system and a two-degree anharmonic system with quartic coefficient lambda=0.2, and checks the standalone CSVR kinetic-energy kernel. A separate fixed two-mode release contrasts direct rescaling, Berendsen, Nosé–Hoover and NHC3 while retaining unmet or unresolved original goals. The remaining six methods are planned.
JSON · Markdown

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — Define the controlled temperature [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/#temperature
Coverage: reading

With kinetic energy K and f active degrees of freedom, the kinetic temperature is T = 2 K / (f k_B). Count constraints and removed center-of-mass motion consistently, and separate thermal motion from streaming. State whether rotational degrees of freedom are included.

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — Equal mean temperature does not imply equal distributions [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/#fluctuations
Coverage: reading

For f independent momentum degrees of freedom with classical quadratic kinetic energy, canonical equilibrium gives 2 K/(k_B T₀) a chi-square distribution with f degrees of freedom. Its mean K is f k_B T₀/2 and variance is f(k_B T₀)²/2. Direct rescaling v ← √(T₀/T) v fixes K immediately after application, removing these fluctuations. CSVR instead uses a stochastic factor to generate fluctuations.

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — Separate sampling from dynamics [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/#dynamics
Coverage: reading

An invariant distribution does not ensure adequate finite-time exploration. Even correct equilibrium sampling can coexist with friction- or collision-induced changes in velocity autocorrelations and diffusion. Assess integration error, heat-bath coupling time and random-seed dependence.

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — CSVR and Langevin: shared canonical targets, distinct correlations [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/
Coverage: reading

The new comparison is limited to small classical systems. CSVR and Langevin use matched OBABO splitting, degrees of freedom, temperature, potential and observation times. Distribution, fluctuations and correlations are separate diagnostics. The earlier BAOAB harmonic results remain in their original release.

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — The stochastic CSVR update and its sign [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/#csvr-exact
Coverage: reading

CSVR evolves the total kinetic energy stochastically and scales all momenta together. The implementation uses the 2007 kinetic-energy SDE and exact propagator, with the signed factor in the 2008 paper. Here h denotes a thermostat substep.
The same Gaussian R determines energy and sign. Momentum flips matter for a few degrees of freedom. Draw S directly from a chi-square law with f−1 degrees, with S=0 at f=1; this avoids the Gamma-construction typo identified by the original author.
dK=\frac{\bar K-K}{\tau}\,dt+2\sqrt{\frac{K\bar K}{f\tau}}\,dWc=e^{-h/\tau},\quad a=\frac{(1-c)\bar K}{f},\quad K^+=\left(\sqrt{cK}+\sqrt a\,R\right)^2+aS,\quad R\sim N(0,1),\quad S\sim\chi^2_{f-1}\alpha=\operatorname{sign}\!\left(\sqrt{cK}+\sqrt a\,R\right)\sqrt{K^+/K},\qquad p_i^+=\alpha p_i
Sources: Canonical sampling through velocity rescaling · Stochastic thermostats: comparison of local and global schemes · Algorithms: stochastic velocity rescaling, author correction note

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — Compare with the same splitting [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/#matched-splitting
Coverage: reading

Both new methods use O(Δt/2)–B(Δt/2)–A(Δt)–B(Δt/2)–O(Δt/2) for MD step Δt: A moves coordinates, B applies forces and O is the thermostat. The CSVR formula uses bath substep h=Δt/2. They share a velocity-Verlet core and differ in the bath updates.
Set τ=(2γ)⁻¹ to match kinetic-energy relaxation for the force-free bath. This τ is not the friction time γ⁻¹. At f=1, signed CSVR has the Langevin transition law; a paired-noise check tests the implementation.
The earlier BAOAB example uses a different B–A–O–A–B splitting. Its release and independent linear reference remain unchanged; the new OBABO references and errors do not replace them.
\tau=(2\gamma)^{-1},\qquad p^+=e^{-\gamma h}p+\sqrt{m k_B T_0(1-e^{-2\gamma h})}\,R_{\rm phys}\quad(f=1)
Sources: Stochastic thermostats: comparison of local and global schemes

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — Three separate questions: distribution, fluctuation and correlation [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/#distribution-fluctuation-correlation
Coverage: reading

Both methods share the static canonical target. Check momentum, kinetic energy and instantaneous-temperature distributions, means and variances. Position references are analytic for harmonic systems and use separate quadrature for the anharmonic case. Matching the mean temperature alone does not check fluctuations.
Dynamic correlations depend on the method and coupling time. Measure position q, momentum p, kinetic energy K and total energy H without requiring agreement between methods. For harmonic Langevin, distinguish the continuous matrix exponential from the OBABO discrete stationary covariance/propagator. Other full-system correlations are measured with uncertainty and timestep dependence.
The exact ρK(t)=exp(−t/τ) reference applies only to the isolated bath. Full harmonic or anharmonic motion exchanges K and U, so that expression is not used as its correlation target.
CDF errors are maxima over predeclared checkpoints: five position/energy points and, for the conditional bath, three quantile points. They are not Kolmogorov–Smirnov suprema over the whole distribution. Full-system correlations use canonical-reference centering and normalization, so finite-step zero-lag values need not equal one exactly.

## Thermostats: temperature control and distributions — Sampling limits and implementation boundaries [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/thermostats/#sampling-and-boundaries
Coverage: reading

Preservation from a canonical initial ensemble and relaxation from temperature-perturbed starts are distinct checks. Use independent replicas, fixed seeds and finite observation windows; separate sampling uncertainty from timestep and coupling effects. These small tests do not guarantee mixing from arbitrary starts. Correlation standard errors use the spread of products across independent replicas at each lag; they are not uncertainties of a single-trajectory time average or an effective-sample-size estimate. No independent dynamical reference is claimed for the anharmonic full-system correlations, which are not presented as having zero error.
A common scaling factor does not directly randomize momentum direction. A correct K distribution cannot rule out restricted sampling from invariant conditions such as zero total momentum in a symmetric system, or from invariant subspaces. The adopted degrees of freedom include no added constraints or removed center-of-mass mode.
For a positive bath step, at K=0 the direction is undefined, so this implementation rejects global rescaling explicitly. It does not inject an arbitrary direction as an undocumented algorithm. Nonfinite or nonphysical parameters are also checked.
Sources: Canonical sampling through velocity rescaling

Coverage: reading

Spatial reconstruction and time integration are independent choices. After spatial discretization, a PDE becomes an ODE system dU/dt = L(U). Accuracy, stability, monotonicity, dissipation, and cost then depend on both parts. The time integration notebook isolates the temporal choice using y′ = i y, y(0) = 1.
THE READING ROOM公開コード・データ / Public code and data

## Time integration and leapfrog — Twelve methods on one oscillator# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/time-integration/#twelve-methods-on-one-oscillator
Coverage: reading

The exact solution exp(i t) follows the unit circle. Forward Euler and backward Euler are first order: the former grows on this undamped oscillator, while the latter damps it. The explicit RK2 family includes Heun / SSPRK(2,2), explicit midpoint, and Ralston. Kutta RK3, SSPRK(3,3), and SSPRK(4,3) are third order; classical RK4 and SSPRK(5,4) are fourth order. Implicit midpoint is second order and preserves the amplitude of this linear oscillator. Its phase still has error. Read the RK family chapter and use the family notebook for stage/order/SSP comparisons and nonlinear tests.
For y′ = lambda y, define z = lambda delta t. One-step amplification factors include
R_{\rm FE}=1+z,\quad R_{\rm BE}=\frac1{1-z},\quad
R_{\rm midpoint}=\frac{1+z/2}{1-z/2}.
The RK factors are the exponential Taylor polynomial through degree two, three, or four for the three RK2 variants, Kutta RK3 / SSPRK(3,3), or classical RK4 on this scalar linear equation. SSPRK(4,3) instead has a degree-four term z⁴/48; SSPRK(5,4) has an additional degree-five term. Shared scalar amplification does not make nonlinear RK stages identical. SSP properties depend on a forward-Euler bound for the spatial operator; they are not unconditional stability.

## Time integration and leapfrog — Leapfrog needs two roots# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/time-integration/#leapfrog-needs-two-roots
Coverage: reading

The centered, two-step first-order-system recurrence is
y^{n+1}=y^{n-1}+2z y^n,\qquad
\xi_\pm=z\pm\sqrt{1+z^2}.
The root tending to +1 as z tends to zero carries the physical mode; the root tending to −1 carries a computational mode alternating between steps. Both roots and their multiplicities matter. For z = i sigma, distinct roots have unit modulus when |sigma| < 1. At |sigma| = 1 the repeated root can give linearly growing solutions; do not include that endpoint in a general boundedness claim. Above it, one root grows geometrically.
A starting value is required in addition to y(0). This implementation takes one RK4 step, optionally adding a real perturbation epsilon to y(1). At lambda = 0 that perturbation gives even samples equal to 1 and odd samples equal to 1+epsilon: a direct computational-mode demonstration. For the notebook’s oscillator it also perturbs the physical mode.
Time filters such as the Robert–Asselin family modify this behavior, with their own damping and accuracy tradeoffs; see Williams (2009). No filter is applied in this edition.

## Time integration and leapfrog — Particle leapfrog is a different formulation# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/time-integration/#particle-leapfrog-is-a-different-formulation
Coverage: reading

A staggered kick–drift scheme for position and velocity, or velocity Verlet for a second-order mechanical system, is often also called leapfrog. Its variables live at different temporal locations and its symplectic interpretation uses that structure. The scalar recurrence above is not a demonstration of a complete SPH particle integrator or a proof of long-time energy conservation for general mechanics.

## Time integration and leapfrog — Reproduce and read the notebook# [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/time-integration/#reproduce-and-read-the-notebook
Coverage: reading

from numart.time_integration import linear_trajectory, leapfrog_roots
t, y = linear_trajectory(rate=1j, dt=0.1, steps=200, method='leapfrog')
print(leapfrog_roots(0.1j))
The browser selects from Python-computed trajectories with fixed final time 20, twelve methods, seven step sizes, and three leapfrog starting perturbations. Axes expand for unstable samples. A matching time interval is not an equal-cost comparison: implicit solves and RK stages differ. Tests measure temporal refinement orders and check the leapfrog roots, alternating mode, and midpoint amplitude. These oscillator trajectories evaluate the scalar stability factor, which is algebraically equivalent to RK stages on this linear test equation; the separate family notebook evaluates full nonlinear stages.
Continue with the spatial stability laboratory, SPH, and ALE.

Methods used

Restarted GMRES
Centered spatial difference
Armijo-damped Newton
Methods used by this fixed-input execution. Their guides describe applicable conditions and the checked scope.
Equations
This example’s formulation and conditions
Formulation, approximation and diagnostic scope
Analytic Jv, Poisson-Thomas right preconditioning and the preserved GMRES body solve tangents/adjoints. Save every rtol, returned candidate, true residual, termination and roundoff scale. Qualify the discrete oracle through shooting and separate high-precision Thomas-Newton. R2 uses a general near-neighbor-difference association in binary64 Jv; the original nonlinear residual,GMRES and tolerances are unchanged. R3 expands only stateNewtoncorrections ashi+lo,direct9productresidual and3productstateupdate. Physicalstates stayfloat64;derivative/adjointGMRES staysordinary.
Bratu nonlinear boundary-value problem
31/63 interior nodes; gaps .1/.01/.001 below the discrete-fold anchor. Every state starts at zero on the lower branch. Parse each lambda string once to binary float; the Decimal oracle evaluates exactly that float.

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-adjoint/
Coverage: reading

The continuum fold is not the discrete fold. rtol1e-4/1e-8 targets are required; requested1e-12 is observational and unmet is never called converged. Independent accuracy of the returned gradient is a separate gate. Eigenvalue/roundoff scales are floating diagnostics, not certified intervals. Bratu J is symmetric; the nonsymmetric transpose is a separate operator control. The retained /solver/gmres/retention_adaptation text is historicalR1/R2;the newcontract explicitly overrides it for mixed-precisionSTATEsolves. ProjectedUNMET is separatelysaved.

## Adjoints through time steps, folds and distributed coefficients — Assumptions, units and boundaries [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-adjoint/#bratu-fold-sensitivity-assumptions
Coverage: reading

31/63 interior nodes; gaps .1/.01/.001 below the discrete-fold anchor. Every state starts at zero on the lower branch. Parse each lambda string once to binary float; the Decimal oracle evaluates exactly that float.

## Adjoints through time steps, folds and distributed coefficients — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-adjoint/#bratu-fold-sensitivity-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Analytic Jv, Poisson-Thomas right preconditioning and the preserved GMRES body solve tangents/adjoints. Save every rtol, returned candidate, true residual, termination and roundoff scale. Qualify the discrete oracle through shooting and separate high-precision Thomas-Newton. R2 uses a general near-neighbor-difference association in binary64 Jv; the original nonlinear residual,GMRES and tolerances are unchanged. R3 expands only stateNewtoncorrections ashi+lo,direct9productresidual and3productstateupdate. Physicalstates stayfloat64;derivative/adjointGMRES staysordinary.
G(u,\lambda)=A_hu-\lambda e^u=0,\quad Js=e^u,\quad J^Tp=hu\mathcal J=\tfrac12h\sum_i u_i^2+0.025\lambda^2,\quad \mathcal J_\lambda=0.05\lambda+p^Te^uq^T(s_D-\hat s)-p_D^Tr=-p_D^Tr_D+r_{p,D}^T(s_D-\hat s)

## Adjoints through time steps, folds and distributed coefficients — References and measured quantities [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-adjoint/#bratu-fold-sensitivity-validation
Coverage: reading

Pre-run freeze:independent67-check reference qualification, then shared32pytest and141fixed group gates. Retain all inputs, tolerances and failures. Actual outcomes are recorded in the bundled result/verification. Initial attempt retained32passing tests and59diffusion/45fold gates before an unmet inner target. R2 general Jv association has separate96component checks; this does not imply primary success. R2 primary failure is also retained. R3 state-onlyhi+lo has separate20component checks;actual three-caseoutcomes are inresult/verification. Fullownership evidence is in the JSONL file/byteoffset/recordSHA referenced by each linear_memory summary;only compact summaries enter case metrics.

## Adjoints through time steps, folds and distributed coefficients — Matrix-free VJP for distributed Bratu coefficients [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-adjoint/
Coverage: reading

Represent8/16/32 spatial controls with two local hat weights per node; compare objective-wise adjoint VJPs with a separate full-sensitivity reference.
Methods, equations, figures and references
Methods used
Implicit differentiation and adjoint methods
Restarted GMRES
Centered spatial difference
Armijo-damped Newton
Methods used by this fixed-input execution. Their guides describe applicable conditions and the checked scope.
Equations
This example’s formulation and conditions
Formulation, approximation and diagnostic scope
Bv uses local gather and B transpose scatter-add. Primary solves use Jv without an n-by-m matrix. One shared Poisson factor serves the one/three-objective runs on the same state. Dense hats and m tangent RHS are allowed only in the separate reference window. R2 uses a general near-neighbor-difference association in binary64 Jv; the original nonlinear residual,GMRES and tolerances are unchanged. R3 expands only stateNewtoncorrections ashi+lo,direct9productresidual and3productstateupdate. Physicalstates stayfloat64;derivative/adjointGMRES staysordinary.
Bratu nonlinear boundary-value problem
63 interior nodes; a(x)=2+B theta with theta=.2sin(2pi xi)+.1cos(pi xi). State/sensitivity have fixed zero Dirichlet endpoints; endpoint coefficient controls are not fixed zero.
Problem figure

## Adjoints through time steps, folds and distributed coefficients — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-adjoint/#bratu-distributed-vjp-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Bv uses local gather and B transpose scatter-add. Primary solves use Jv without an n-by-m matrix. One shared Poisson factor serves the one/three-objective runs on the same state. Dense hats and m tangent RHS are allowed only in the separate reference window. R2 uses a general near-neighbor-difference association in binary64 Jv; the original nonlinear residual,GMRES and tolerances are unchanged. R3 expands only stateNewtoncorrections ashi+lo,direct9productresidual and3productstateupdate. Physicalstates stayfloat64;derivative/adjointGMRES staysordinary.
G=A_hu-(2+B\theta)e^u,\quad J^Tp=q,\quad \nabla_\theta\mathcal J=B^T(e^u\odot p)a_{\rm endpoints}=[a-b,a+b],\quad\theta_{\rm endpoints}=[a-b-2,a+b-2]

Run inside atlas-approximation-controls-2026-11-25 from the ZIP. This command executes all 3 fixed cases in the supplement. The bundled results/ contains stored outputs. Rerun into a new output/ directory, and choose another fresh directory for subsequent runs.
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pytest -q
python run.py --input inputs.json --output output
Matplotlib is optional for redrawing saved figures; ordinary scientific execution does not require it.

## Fixed interpolation, spline and Haar controls — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-approximation-controls/#runge-barycentric-clenshaw-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Implement the second barycentric formula and a full-coefficient Clenshaw recurrence. Retain the closed weights and finite Chebyshev transform on rounded nodes.
p(x)=sum_j y_j*prod_(k!=j)((x-x_k)/(x_j-x_k))R(x)=(sum_j w_j*y_j/(x-x_j))/(sum_j w_j/(x-x_j))C(x)=sum_(k=0)^n a_k*T_k(x); b_k=a_k+2*x*b_(k+1)-b_(k+2)

Compare C2 continuity and shape preservation on three fixed data sets: a monotone plateau, a cubic and a straight line.
Methods, equations, figures and references
Methods used
Spline interpolation
PCHIP monotone cubic Hermite interpolation
Methods used by this fixed-input execution. Their guides describe applicable conditions and the checked scope.
Equations
This example’s formulation and conditions
Solve a cubic B-spline collocation system and evaluate it with de Boor recursion. A separate path implements PCHIP harmonic slopes, endpoint limiting and Hermite evaluation.
Cubic splines and shape-preserving interpolation
Use actual binary64 knots and values. Natural conditions set both endpoint second derivatives to zero; clamped conditions prescribe the first derivatives from the input.

Exact / reference solutions
References and checks for this execution
Reference and validation scope
Compare with exact rational second-derivative systems, rational PCHIP and SciPy 1.14.1. Fifteen endpoint records contain sixteen scalar outputs from thirteen distinct inputs. Independent Fraction formulas show plateau undershoot for the actual binary64 data.

## Fixed interpolation, spline and Haar controls — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-approximation-controls/#spline-shape-controls-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Solve a cubic B-spline collocation system and evaluate it with de Boor recursion. A separate path implements PCHIP harmonic slopes, endpoint limiting and Hermite evaluation.
S_i(s)=a_i+b_i*s+c_i*s^2+d_i*s^3d_k=(w_1+w_2)/(w_1/m_(k-1)+w_2/m_k)S_natural(1.5)=a-9*(b-a)/88; S_clamped(1.5)=a-15*(b-a)/152

## Fixed interpolation, spline and Haar controls — Assumptions, units and boundaries [en]

At each odd-length level append the first sample for periodic extension or the last for symmetric extension, then crop during synthesis. Apply threshold 0.2 only to detail coefficients.

## Fixed interpolation, spline and Haar controls — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-approximation-controls/#haar-mallat-boundary-threshold-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Implement pair-sum and pair-difference filters, downsampling and inverse pyramids. Reconstruct with no threshold, hard thresholding and soft thresholding from the same analysis coefficients.
a_(l+1,k)=(a_(l,2k)+a_(l,2k+1))/sqrt(2)d_(l+1,k)=(a_(l,2k)-a_(l,2k+1))/sqrt(2)E_after=E_before+padding^2; ||e||_2^2=||delta_coeff||_2^2 only for square orthogonal transform

## Biological reaction–diffusion: two-dimensional and boundary controls — Download and execute the supplement [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology-space-controls/#run-all
Coverage: reading

Run inside atlas-biology-space-controls-2026-11-25 from the ZIP. This command executes all 3 fixed cases in the supplement. The bundled results/ contains stored outputs. Rerun into a new output/ directory, and choose another fresh directory for subsequent runs.
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pytest -q
python run.py --input inputs.json --output output
Matplotlib is optional for redrawing saved figures; ordinary scientific execution does not require it.

## Biological reaction–diffusion: two-dimensional and boundary controls — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology-space-controls/#fisher-kpp-special-front-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Use centered second-order differences and SSPRK3 with exact Dirichlet values at every stage. Compare time errors to an independent reference for the same95-unknown semidiscreteODE.

## Biological reaction–diffusion: two-dimensional and boundary controls — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology-space-controls/#schnakenberg-2d-boundary-modes-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Strang-split cell-averageCN diffusion and local implicit-midpoint reactions. Independent orthonormal sine/cosine Galerkin references retain four K12/18,Q96/192,tolerance rows for every initial condition. The original Dirichlet K12/18 reference failed its first relative qualification. Preserve that failure and add four D-only K24/32,Q128/192 reference actions.

## Independent validation of nonlinear reaction–diffusion and pattern formation — Finite-amplitude Schnakenberg transient: nonlinearity and independent reference [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology/
Coverage: reading

Compare raw L1/L2/L∞ with a spatially independent cosine Fourier–Galerkin/Radau reference (K32/64/96, cubic projection M=4(K+1)>4K, analytic Jacobian). Separately check K and ODE-tolerance sensitivity. Measure time order against a separately implemented Radau integration of the SAME FD semidiscretization. Norms are per-species mean-absolute/RMS/maximum, then the worse species. Record source/sink balance, every-step positive concentrations, initially absent k≥5 (first allowed k6 here), and departure from linearization. Convergence norms and reference sensitivities are assessed at the fixed final time; intermediate snapshot errors are separate evolution diagnostics.
No corresponding reference-library card is registered. The execution-specific validation material above documents its reference values and acceptance checks.
Input and validation protocol history · Initial input

## Independent validation of nonlinear reaction–diffusion and pattern formation — Assumptions, units and boundaries [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology/#schnakenberg-nonlinear-assumptions
Coverage: reading

1D periodic x∈[0,2π), a=.1,b=.9,D=(.01,1). Common IC u=1+.08cos(2x)+.01cos(4x), v=.9−.03cos(2x)−.002cos(4x), restricted to a reflection-even, pi-periodic invariant subspace with a fixed origin.

## Independent validation of nonlinear reaction–diffusion and pattern formation — Adopted numerical method [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology/#schnakenberg-nonlinear-algorithm
Coverage: reading

Strang-compose exact half-step diffusion of the FD matrix, diagonalized by FFT with symbol −4sin²(πk/N)/dx², and a full implicit-midpoint reaction step solved by local2×2 Newton iterations. FFT does not change FD space into spectral space. Fail on nonconvergence/budget excess; never clip concentrations.
u_t=D_u u_{xx}+a-u+u^2v,\qquad v_t=D_v v_{xx}+b-u^2v\frac{d\langle u+v\rangle}{dt}=a+b-\langle u\rangle,\quad S_{n+1}-S_n=h(a+b-\langle\bar u\rangle)\lambda_{h,k}=-4\sin^2(\pi k/N)/\Delta x^2,\quad\Phi_h=e^{hDL_h/2}\,\Phi_{\rm midpoint}^{F}(h)\,e^{hDL_h/2}\|e\|_1=\max_s\frac1N\sum_j|e_{s,j}|,\quad\|e\|_2=\max_s\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_j e_{s,j}^2},\quad\|e\|_\infty=\max_{s,j}|e_{s,j}|

## Independent validation of nonlinear reaction–diffusion and pattern formation — References and measured quantities [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology/#schnakenberg-nonlinear-validation
Coverage: reading

Compare raw L1/L2/L∞ with a spatially independent cosine Fourier–Galerkin/Radau reference (K32/64/96, cubic projection M=4(K+1)>4K, analytic Jacobian). Separately check K and ODE-tolerance sensitivity. Measure time order against a separately implemented Radau integration of the SAME FD semidiscretization. Norms are per-species mean-absolute/RMS/maximum, then the worse species. Record source/sink balance, every-step positive concentrations, initially absent k≥5 (first allowed k6 here), and departure from linearization. Convergence norms and reference sensitivities are assessed at the fixed final time; intermediate snapshot errors are separate evolution diagnostics.

## Independent validation of nonlinear reaction–diffusion and pattern formation — Verification limits and failures [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology/#schnakenberg-nonlinear-limits
Coverage: reading

A selected-symmetry1D educational model: no test of free noise-driven wavenumber selection, phase stability,2D spots or biological calibration. Not an original-paper reproduction. Implicit midpoint is A-stable but not L-stable or unconditionally positive; reactions do not conserve u+v. The initial coarse protocol failed; temporal resolution was strengthened while retaining every acceptance threshold and the failed record. No quantum calculations.

## Independent validation of nonlinear reaction–diffusion and pattern formation — Primary sources and review scope [en]

Source: https://hrkoyama.github.io/numerical-methods-atlas/en/read/validation-biology/#schnakenberg-nonlinear-references
Coverage: reading

Bibliography, abstracts, selected original sections and executed official code have distinct review scopes. Full papers and third-party code are not reproduced wholesale, and no blanket full-text audit is claimed.
A. M. Turing (1952). The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis · DOI: 10.1098/rstb.1952.0012
Review scope / review_level: original-paper-selected-sections
Checked the university-hosted original scan, sections 6–7 (printed pp.46–50), ring formulation/linearization and bibliography. Distinct from the adopted coefficients, finite-amplitude reference and mature shape.
J. Schnakenberg (1979). Simple chemical reaction systems with limit cycle behaviour · DOI: 10.1016/0022-5193(79)90042-0
Review scope / review_level: official-bibliography-and-publisher-indexed-abstract
Checked official PubMed bibliography/DOI and publisher-indexed abstract. Full text returned403. Historical source for the reaction family, not a claim to reproduce original coefficients or experiments.
G. Strang (1968). On the Construction and Comparison of Difference Schemes · DOI: 10.1137/0705041
Review scope / review_level: original-paper-selected-nonlinear-composition
Checked original pp.510–512 for half-step composition and nonlinear second-order construction. This does not guarantee positivity or accuracy at arbitrary steps in the adopted model.
E. Hairer (2010). Geometric Numerical Integration, Lecture2

Coverage: reading

Review scope / review_level: author-lecture-selected-midpoint-and-splitting
Checked theorem3 and section5 of the author-hosted lecture for implicit-midpoint formula/order and symmetric splitting. Hamiltonian symplectic claims are not transferred to this chemical model.
The SciPy community (2024). SciPy1.14.1 solve_ivp and Radau reference
Review scope / review_level: official-versioned-api-specification
Checked official Radau IIA order5, local rtol/atol scaling, analytic Jacobians and termination status. ODE tolerances do not certify global continuum-PDE accuracy.
